tema: Diagnostic + Mission Briefing — Reading the ASON Exam Through Helena's Eyes
homework: Task 1 (20 min): Download the ASON 2026 English exam (teacher provides PDF link). Read only the texts — do not answer the questions yet. Highlight every word or phrase you do not fully understand. Bring the annotated PDF to Lesson 2. Task 2 (10 min): Write a list of exactly 10 maritime words you already know in English (any source — previous exams, research, intuition). No dictionary allowed. This list will be compared against the program vocabulary map in Lesson 2 to measure your existing baseline. Submit both items via shared Google Drive folder before the next lesson.
atividadeEmAula: Phase 1 (10 min) — Lead-in: Teacher shares screen with a single image of a merchant vessel bridge and asks Helena to describe what she sees in English, unprompted. Teacher notes fluency, vocabulary range, and confidence level without interrupting. This is the spoken baseline. Phase 2 (20 min) — Diagnostic Reading Task 1: Teacher shares a 250-word adapted excerpt from the ASON 2025 exam (text about COLREGS — collision regulations at sea). Helena reads silently, then answers 4 multiple-choice questions modeled exactly on the ASON format. Teacher observes: Does she self-correct? Does she re-read? Does she flag unknown words? Phase 3 (20 min) — Diagnostic Reading Task 2: A second text (150 words) on basic ship types and cargo classification. Helena answers 3 questions and then — crucially — is asked to verbally explain why she chose each answer. Teacher maps her reasoning process: is she guessing, scanning, or truly comprehending? Phase 4 (15 min) — Gap Mapping: Teacher and Helena co-build a visual 'gap map' on screen (shared Google Doc) identifying: words she did not recognize, question types that caused hesitation, and patterns she noticed across both texts. Helena's own strategic analysis is activated here — she has compared exam editions before, so this is familiar territory. Phase 5 (15 min) — Program Overview: Teacher walks Helena through the 38-lesson roadmap, explains the 60/40 maritime/general split, and frames the curriculum as mission preparation — not language learning in the abstract. The ASON exam date (last week of March 2027) is placed on a shared timeline. Helena sees exactly where she is and where she needs to be. Phase 6 (10 min) — Wrap-up: Teacher summarizes the three confirmed gaps (maritime vocabulary, reading speed under pressure, technical register familiarity) and previews Lesson 2. Helena confirms or adjusts the priority ranking.
focoLinguistico: Diagnostic focus: no new grammar introduced as content. Assessment targets: (1) reading comprehension of technical maritime texts — ability to identify main idea, infer meaning from context, handle unfamiliar vocabulary; (2) passive recognition of maritime vocabulary (vessel, navigation, cargo, port, crew, bridge, hull, draft, knot, nautical mile); (3) grammar processing in context — modal verbs, passive voice, conditional structures as they appear in exam texts. Vocabulary circulating (diagnostic baseline): vessel, navigation, cargo, port, crew, bridge, hull, draft, knot, nautical mile (10 words — all maritime core, assessed not taught). Expressions assessed: stand by (be ready), cast off (leave the dock), on board (aboard), underway (moving), at berth (docked).

tema: The Ship's World — Core Maritime Vocabulary and How the ASON Tests It
homework: Task 1 (25 min): Using the ASON 2026 exam PDF (already annotated), now answer all the English questions you had NOT answered before. Do not use a dictionary. Submit your answers with a short note (2-3 sentences in English) explaining which question was hardest and why. Task 2 (15 min): Create 10 flashcards (using Quizlet or a shared Google Doc) for today's new vocabulary. Each card: word on front, English definition plus one sentence from a ship context on back. Share the deck link in the Google Drive folder. Estimated total time: 40 minutes.
atividadeEmAula: Phase 1 (10 min) — Warm-up: Helena shares her annotated ASON 2026 exam PDF (homework Task 1). Teacher and Helena do a rapid 3-minute scan together: teacher asks Helena to point out the three words she highlighted most confidently as unknown. These three words anchor the vocabulary presentation. Phase 2 (18 min) — Presentation: Teacher introduces the 10 new vocabulary words using a ship diagram on screen (labeled vessel blueprint — shareable image). Each word is shown in context with a sentence pulled directly from real ASON-style exam texts, not invented examples. Modal perfects are introduced by showing how they appear in answer options: 'The officer must have been unaware of the regulation' vs 'The officer may have indicated a different course.' Teacher shows how the modal shifts the certainty level and how that changes which answer is correct. Phase 3 (17 min) — Practice: Vocabulary matching activity (shared Google Form): Helena matches 10 new words to their definitions (in English only, no Portuguese). Then a second round: 5 sentences from ASON-style texts where she identifies which modal perfect is correct and why. Teacher monitors live and pauses to discuss any hesitations. Phase 4 (35 min) — Production (reading-focused at B2): Teacher shares a full 300-word maritime text about pilotage services in international ports (ASON-register). Helena reads and answers 5 multiple-choice questions. After answering, she must explain each choice aloud using the reasoning pattern: 'I chose B because the text says X, which means Y.' Teacher coaches the reasoning verbalization — this is not just comprehension, it is exam technique. Final 10 minutes: Helena and teacher re-read the two answer choices she found hardest and identify whether the difficulty was vocabulary, grammar, or text structure. Phase 5 (10 min) — Wrap-up: Teacher adds today's 10 words to the shared vocabulary tracker (Google Sheet). Helena rates her confidence on each word: 1 (new), 2 (seen before), 3 (I can use it). Ratings guide next lesson's revision selection.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Foundation — new): Modal perfects in reading context — must have been, could have been, may have indicated — as they appear in exam answer choices and distractor options. Understanding how modal perfects shift meaning in technical sentences is a direct exam skill. New vocabulary (10 words): starboard (right side of ship), port side (left side of ship), bow (front), stern (rear), keel (bottom structural spine), ballast (weight used for stability), manifest (cargo document), pilot (navigation officer), berth (docking space or bunk), waypoint (navigation checkpoint). Revision from Lesson 1 (3 words): vessel, draft, underway. Expressions (new): take the helm (assume control), lay anchor (stop and anchor), clear for departure (authorized to leave port), on watch (on duty shift), log entry (official record). Collocations: navigate a route, maintain a course, issue a report, comply with regulations.

tema: Rules of the Sea — Reading COLREGS and IMO Language at ASON Level
homework: Task 1 (20 min): Read COLREGS Rules 13, 14, and 15 in English (teacher provides PDF — official IMO text, short version). Highlight every instance of reported speech or regulation language ('shall,' 'must,' 'is required to'). Write 3 sentences in English summarizing what each rule means in your own words — do not copy the text. Task 2 (10 min): Review your Quizlet deck from Lesson 2 and add today's 10 new words. For each new word, write one sentence connecting it to a real navigation scenario (e.g., 'The give-way vessel altered course to avoid a collision near the traffic separation scheme'). Submit via shared Google Drive. Estimated total time: 30 minutes.
atividadeEmAula: Phase 1 (10 min) — Warm-up: Teacher displays a simplified COLREGS diagram on screen (Rule 15 — crossing situation: give-way vs stand-on vessel). Without vocabulary input yet, Helena explains in English what she thinks is happening in the diagram. Teacher notes which technical terms she reaches for and which she cannot access — this activates schema and reveals gaps before the lesson begins. Phase 2 (18 min) — Presentation: Teacher introduces the 10 new words through 3 authentic-register sentences from COLREGS Rule 8, Rule 16, and Rule 17 (simplified but not distorted). Each sentence is displayed on screen, the target word is highlighted, and Helena is asked to infer the meaning before the definition is given — consistent with the reading strategy she needs for the exam. Reported speech is then shown as a structural pattern in real exam sentences: teacher places two versions of the same information side by side (direct vs reported) and asks Helena to identify which version appears in exam texts. Phase 3 (17 min) — Practice: Teacher shares a 200-word ASON-style passage about a crossing situation at sea. The text contains 4 instances of reported speech and 6 of the new vocabulary words. Helena reads and completes two tasks simultaneously: (1) underline every reported speech structure; (2) circle every new vocabulary word. Then answers 4 multiple-choice questions. Teacher and Helena review answer by answer, with Helena explaining her reasoning aloud. Phase 4 (35 min) — Production: Timed reading simulation. Teacher shares a 320-word text (ASON 2025 exam difficulty level, real maritime regulation context). Helena has exactly 12 minutes to read and answer 5 questions — simulating the actual time pressure of the exam. After the timer ends, teacher and Helena debrief: Which questions were answered confidently? Which required re-reading? Was there a vocabulary gap or a grammar gap? Teacher introduces the 'anchor word' strategy: find the one word in the text that confirms or eliminates each answer option. Helena practices applying it on 2 of the 5 questions retroactively. Phase 5 (10 min) — Wrap-up: Vocabulary tracker updated. Helena identifies her 3 weakest words from today and commits to a specific review method (flashcard, sentence writing, or re-reading in context) before next lesson.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Foundation — new): Reported speech (complete — all tenses) as it appears in technical maritime documentation and exam texts. ASON texts frequently report what regulations state, what officers declared, what the manual specifies. Mastering reported speech as a reading tool — not a production tool — is essential for answer accuracy. Examples from ASON register: 'The regulation states that vessels must maintain a safe speed,' 'The officer reported that visibility had deteriorated,' 'The manual indicated that the procedure should be followed.' New vocabulary (10 words): collision (impact between vessels), visibility (how far you can see), give-way vessel (vessel required to yield), stand-on vessel (vessel with right of way), restricted waters (narrow or shallow areas), lookout (person watching for hazards), sound signal (horn/whistle communication), distress (emergency state), anchor watch (monitoring while anchored), traffic separation scheme (organized maritime traffic lanes). Revision from Lesson 2 (2 words): starboard, bow. Expressions (new): keep clear of (stay away from), alter course (change direction), sound one short blast (give one horn signal — COLREGS language), in compliance with (following the rules), as prescribed by (as required by a regulation). Collocations: report an incident, observe a regulation, maintain a safe distance, declare an emergency.

tema: Cargo, Ports, and Ship Operations — The Technical Register of Maritime Commerce
homework: Task 1 (20 min): Find and read any real bill of lading document in English (teacher provides a sample PDF). Identify at least 8 words or phrases from today's lesson that appear in the document. Write 3 sentences in English describing what the document is for, what it contains, and why it matters on a merchant vessel. Task 2 (15 min): Complete a passive voice transformation exercise (teacher provides 10-item Google Form): each item gives an active sentence about maritime operations; Helena rewrites it in passive voice and, where possible, in causative form. Submit via Google Form — results auto-shared with teacher. Estimated total time: 35 minutes.
atividadeEmAula: Phase 1 (10 min) — Warm-up: Teacher shares a short port operations infographic on screen showing cargo flow from origin to vessel. Helena narrates the sequence in English, using any vocabulary she already has. Teacher notes where she pauses — these moments become anchor points for the vocabulary presentation. Phase 2 (18 min) — Presentation: Teacher displays three authentic-register sentences from ASON-type texts featuring standard passive and causative structures. Side-by-side comparison on screen: 'The cargo was inspected by the port authority' (passive) vs 'The captain had the cargo inspected by the port authority' (causative). Teacher asks Helena to identify the difference in meaning — who initiated the action. This distinction is shown to matter in multiple-choice answer options where one option uses causative and the other uses standard passive with a different implied agent. The 10 new vocabulary words are introduced through a bill of lading template displayed on screen — all terms appear in their natural document context, not in isolation. Phase 3 (17 min) — Practice: Teacher shares a 220-word ASON-style text about port clearance procedures. Task 1: Helena identifies every passive or causative structure and rewrites the sentence identifying the agent. Task 2: Helena answers 4 comprehension questions and identifies which vocabulary words were essential to getting the right answer. Teacher debriefs each answer with the question: 'What was the key word that confirmed this answer?' Phase 4 (35 min) — Production: Full ASON-format simulation with two texts. Text A (180 words): cargo inspection at a Brazilian port. Text B (200 words): container ship loading operations. Helena has 14 minutes total for both texts and 6 questions. After the timed session, teacher and Helena do a full forensic debrief: for every wrong or uncertain answer, they trace the exact sentence in the text where the correct answer was hidden. Teacher introduces the 'distractor anatomy' concept — how ASON multiple-choice distractors are built (partially true, reverse causality, wrong agent in passive). Helena examines 2 real distractor options from the 2025 exam. Phase 5 (10 min) — Wrap-up: Helena adds today's words to vocabulary tracker with confidence ratings. Teacher previews Lesson 5: a full timed simulation with debrief — the first complete mock exam experience of the program.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Building — new): Passive voice advanced — causative 'have something done' and standard passive in technical maritime texts. ASON exam texts consistently describe operations in passive voice ('The cargo was inspected,' 'The vessel was cleared for departure,' 'Maintenance was carried out'). Causative structures appear in operational contexts: 'The captain had the cargo inspected before departure,' 'The port authority had the documents verified.' Reading these structures accurately — and not confusing passive with active in answer options — is a direct exam skill. New vocabulary (10 words): freight (cargo being transported commercially), consignment (a batch of goods being shipped), bill of lading (official cargo document), port authority (body controlling port operations), clearance (official authorization to proceed), loading (putting cargo on the ship), unloading/discharge (removing cargo), stowage (arranging cargo in the hold), hold (interior cargo space of a ship), gross tonnage (measurement of ship's total enclosed volume). Revision from Lesson 3 (3 words): manifest, berth, distress. Expressions (new): clear customs (pass official inspection), take on cargo (load goods), off-load (discharge cargo), in transit (being transported), subject to inspection (must be inspected). Phrasal verbs (new): carry out (inspection, procedure), phase out (old equipment), account for (explain discrepancies in cargo documentation).

tema: Full ASON Simulation — Timed Exam Practice and Strategic Debrief (End of Block 1)
homework: Task 1 (30 min): Review the Block 1 Progress Summary document (teacher shares after lesson). For every vocabulary word you rated 1 (new/uncertain) in any lesson, write one original English sentence using that word in a maritime context. Minimum 10 sentences. Submit via shared Google Drive before Lesson 6. Task 2 (20 min): Read a short article from MarineInsight.com or Splash247.com (your choice of topic — any maritime subject). Write 5 sentences in English summarizing what you read, using at least 5 vocabulary words from Block 1. This is your first independent exposure task — note any new maritime words you encounter that were not in the lessons and bring them to Lesson 6. Estimated total time: 50 minutes.
atividadeEmAula: Phase 1 (10 min) — Warm-up: Quick vocabulary sprint — teacher displays 15 words from Lessons 1-4 on screen one by one (5 seconds each). Helena gives a one-word English definition or uses the word in a phrase. No pressure scoring — this is activation, not testing. Teacher notes which words still feel unstable. Phase 2 (18 min) — Presentation: Inversion in formal maritime writing. Teacher shows 4 sentences on screen — two normal word order, two inverted — both from ASON-difficulty texts. Helena identifies which is which. Teacher explains the grammar pattern (auxiliary moved before subject) and why it appears in formal/legal English. Then: 3 real inverted structures from IMO-register texts, with comprehension questions attached — Helena practices reading them for meaning, not for production. New vocabulary introduced through two authentic contexts: a brief incident report template (master, manning, watchkeeping, STCW, ISM Code) and a safety drill scenario (muster station, lifeboat drill, render assistance, proceed to). Phase 3 (17 min) — Practice: Teacher shares a 180-word incident report in English (ASON-register). The text contains 2 inverted structures and 7 of today's new vocabulary words. Helena answers 4 comprehension questions and identifies every inverted structure. Then: teacher shows 3 distractor pairs from real ASON exams and Helena explains which answer is wrong and exactly why — naming the distractor type (wrong agent, partial truth, or reverse causality, from the taxonomy introduced in Lesson 4). Phase 4 (35 min) — Full ASON Simulation (End of Block 1 Assessment): Teacher shares a complete 4-text, 10-question ASON-format English exam built from authentic-register maritime texts at 2025-2026 difficulty. Helena completes the full exam under timed conditions: 30 minutes for reading and answering, no interruptions, teacher observes silently. Texts cover: port operations, COLREGS, cargo documentation, and crew safety regulations — all four content areas covered in Block 1. After the timer: teacher and Helena review all 10 answers together. For each question: (1) Was it right or wrong? (2) What was the key sentence in the text? (3) If wrong: was the gap vocabulary, grammar, or reading strategy? Teacher produces a written Block 1 Progress Summary (shared Google Doc) with Helena's current baseline score, gap profile, and the three priority areas for Block 2. Phase 5 (10 min) — Wrap-up: Helena reflects aloud: what has changed since Lesson 1? What feels more manageable? What still feels uncertain? Teacher anchors the debrief in the mission — every word Helena now recognizes is one less obstacle between her and the first day of the formation course. Block 2 preview: navigation instruments, meteorology at sea, and STCW deep dive.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Building — new): Inversion for emphasis as it appears in formal maritime and regulatory texts — 'Never should a vessel enter restricted waters without clearance,' 'Not only did the officer fail to maintain a lookout, but he also neglected to log the incident,' 'Hardly had the vessel cleared the harbor when visibility dropped.' ASON texts at higher difficulty use formal inversion in regulation summaries and incident reports. Recognizing inversion in reading (not producing it) is the exam skill target. New vocabulary (10 words): incident report (official account of an event at sea), near miss (almost-collision or almost-accident), master (official title of the ship's captain), flag state (country where ship is registered), manning (having sufficient crew), watchkeeping (maintaining a duty watch), STCW (Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping — IMO convention), ISM Code (International Safety Management — safety regulation framework), muster station (emergency assembly point), lifeboat drill (safety exercise for emergency evacuation). Revision from Lesson 4 (3 words): clearance, freight, stowage). Expressions (new): stand by for inspection (prepare for official check), take command (assume control of the vessel), in accordance with STCW (following international standards), render assistance (help another vessel in distress), proceed to muster station (go to emergency assembly point). Full vocabulary circulating this lesson: 10 new + 3 revision = 13 words.

tema: Navigating ASON Texts — Cleft Sentences and Relative Clauses in Maritime Regulation Language
homework: Task 1 (20 min): Helena reads a 2-paragraph excerpt from the actual SOLAS Convention Chapter V (Safety of Navigation), available at imo.org. She identifies and underlines: (a) all relative clauses — defining and non-defining; (b) any cleft sentence structures. She writes the list in a shared Google Doc with the clause type labeled beside each sentence. Task 2 (15 min): Helena writes 5 original sentences using today's vocabulary — one each for: compliance, liability, jurisdiction, provision, enforcement — all in a maritime context. Each sentence must include either a relative clause or a cleft structure. She sends the Doc before the next lesson.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher shares screen with two authentic ASON-style sentences — one cleft, one standard — and asks Helena to identify which feels more formal and why. Discussion anchors the grammar target in exam register. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents cleft sentences and non-defining relative clauses using a slide built from real IMO document language (SOLAS, STCW). Each example uses vocabulary from today's lesson — compliance, liability, jurisdiction. Helena reads each sentence aloud and reformulates it in standard word order to feel the emphasis shift. Teacher highlights how ASON distractors exploit these structures by placing the cleft clause next to the wrong referent. Practice (17 min): Helena receives a split-screen activity — left column has 6 regulation-style sentences with cleft or relative structures; right column has 4 multiple-choice comprehension questions modeled on the ASON format. She answers independently (8 min), then teacher reviews each answer with explicit explanation of why each distractor is wrong — focusing on clause attachment errors. Production (35 min): Teacher shares a 3-paragraph excerpt from a simulated port authority incident report (teacher-created, ASON-register). Helena reads the full text (5 min), then answers 5 comprehension questions (15 min) under mild time pressure (timer visible on screen). Debrief (15 min): Teacher and Helena go through each answer, identifying which sentence structures appeared — cleft, relative, passive, inversion from Lesson 5 — building Helena's structural recognition map. Wrap-up (10 min): Helena verbally summarizes 3 new vocabulary items in her own definition — compliance, liability, jurisdiction — without looking at notes.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Building — new): Cleft sentences for emphasis in formal maritime texts — 'It was the master who authorized the departure,' 'What the regulation requires is a complete lookout at all times,' 'It is the flag state that bears responsibility for compliance.' Non-defining and defining relative clauses with prepositions at the end — 'The officer, who had been on watch for six hours, failed to log the incident,' 'The port authority to which the vessel was registered issued a warning,' 'The muster station that the crew proceeded to was on deck four.' ASON exam skill: recognizing which clause modifies which noun — a common distractor strategy in multiple-choice comprehension questions. New vocabulary (10 words): compliance (adherence to rules and regulations), liability (legal responsibility for an incident), jurisdiction (legal authority over a maritime zone), amendment (official change to a regulation or document), ratification (formal approval of an international agreement), annex (supplementary section of an official document), convention (international regulatory agreement — as in SOLAS Convention), protocol (set of official rules or procedures), provision (specific clause within a regulation), enforcement (act of ensuring a rule is followed). Revision from Lessons 3 and 5 (3 words): flag state, ISM Code, in compliance with. Collocations (new): fall under jurisdiction, be subject to liability, enforce a provision, ratify a convention, comply with an amendment. Phrasal verbs (new): set out (as in 'The convention sets out the responsibilities of flag states'), come under (as in 'This vessel comes under the jurisdiction of Panama'). Expressions (new): as set forth in (as officially stated in a document), without prejudice to (not affecting the validity of another rule), by virtue of (because of an official status or right).

tema: Reading ASON Under Pressure — Gerunds, Infinitives, and Meaning Shifts in Technical Procedure Language
homework: Task 1 (20 min): Helena reads a 1-page safety procedure extract from an ISM Code-compliant Ship Safety Management Manual (teacher provides PDF via shared Google Drive — sourced from publicly available vessel SMS documents). She identifies all gerund and infinitive verb forms in the text and labels each one in the margin: G (gerund) or INF (infinitive). She notes any pair where the opposite form would change the operational meaning. Task 2 (15 min): Helena writes a 10-sentence officer checklist for a fictional lifeboat drill procedure, using at least 6 of today's vocabulary words and at least 3 gerund-infinitive structures (minimum one meaning-shift pair). She submits via Google Doc before the next lesson.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher shares two authentic-register sentences on screen — 'The officer stopped checking the radar' vs. 'The officer stopped to check the radar' — and asks Helena which version would put the vessel at greater risk and why. The scenario anchors the meaning-shift in operational stakes, not abstract grammar. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents the 4 core gerund-infinitive pairs using a visual two-column slide — left column shows the sentence, right column shows the operational consequence of choosing the wrong form. Helena reads each pair and paraphrases the operational meaning difference in her own words. Teacher then shows 3 actual ASON-style answer choices where the gerund-infinitive distinction is the distractor mechanism. Practice (17 min): Helena completes a 10-item gap-fill drawn from officer procedure logs and maritime incident reports — she must choose the correct verb form (gerund or infinitive) and in 4 items, she must also explain why the other option is operationally wrong. Teacher monitors via shared screen and annotates errors live. Production (35 min): Teacher presents a full simulated ASON reading passage (280 words) about a vessel deviation incident — the text contains gerund-infinitive structures, reported speech from Lesson 3, passive voice from Lesson 4, and today's vocabulary (procedure, malfunction, deviation, contingency, checklist). Helena reads the passage and answers 5 multiple-choice questions (20 min, timer set). Debrief (15 min): Teacher walks through each question, identifying the grammar or vocabulary lever that each distractor exploits. Helena names the structure involved in each wrong answer — building a personal distractor taxonomy. Wrap-up (10 min): Helena defines 4 vocabulary items — alert, hazard, deviation, precaution — using one sentence each, connecting them to a single invented scenario aboard a ship.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Building — new): Gerunds vs. infinitives with meaning shifts as they appear in technical maritime procedure language — the pairs that change meaning are the exam risk. Core pairs: 'stop doing' (cease an activity) vs. 'stop to do' (pause in order to do something); 'remember doing' (recall a past action) vs. 'remember to do' (not forget a future obligation); 'try doing' (experiment with a method) vs. 'try to do' (attempt with difficulty); 'regret doing' (feel sorry about a past action) vs. 'regret to inform' (formal notification of bad news — high frequency in maritime correspondence and ASON texts). Exam skill: ASON uses these pairs in procedure descriptions and officer communications where one option is grammatically correct and the other changes the operational meaning entirely. New vocabulary (10 words): procedure (official step-by-step operational sequence), malfunction (equipment failure), alert (official notification of danger or emergency), deviation (departure from a planned route or approved procedure), contingency (backup plan for an emergency), drill (practice exercise for an emergency procedure), hazard (source of danger on board), checklist (official list of steps to verify), precaution (action taken to prevent an incident), notification (formal communication of an event or decision). Revision from Lesson 4 (3 words): carry out, clearance, discharge. Collocations (new): conduct a drill, issue an alert, follow a procedure, identify a hazard, take a precaution, respond to a malfunction. Phrasal verbs (new): carry out (a drill — recycled with new collocational pair), look into (investigate a malfunction), put forward (a contingency plan). Hedging language introduced (Expansion preview — passive recognition only): 'It would appear that the deviation was unintentional,' 'The report suggests that the malfunction may have occurred prior to departure.'

tema: The Language of Maritime Safety — SOLAS, Emergency Protocols, and Expansion Grammar in ASON Texts
homework: Task 1 (25 min): Helena reads Chapter III of SOLAS (Life-Saving Appliances and Arrangements) — a 1-page summary version provided by teacher via Google Drive. She identifies: (a) all future perfect or future continuous structures; (b) any 'used to / be used to / get used to' patterns; (c) 5 new vocabulary items from today's lesson in context. She annotates directly in the PDF using the comment tool and shares with teacher. Task 2 (10 min): Helena writes 5 sentences describing what will have happened by the time a fictional vessel completes a 7-day voyage — using future perfect. She uses at least 3 vocabulary items from today's lesson. Submission via shared Doc.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher shares a short operational order on screen: 'By 0800, all crew will have reported to their muster stations. The safety officer will be conducting the roll call at that time.' Helena identifies the two future structures and explains the timing difference without prompting. Teacher confirms and connects to the ASON reading skill: choosing between future perfect and simple future in answer options requires understanding whether the action is complete or ongoing at a future reference point. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents future perfect and future continuous using a visual timeline with a vessel voyage as the anchor — departure, transit, arrival, and events at each stage described using both structures. Then 'used to / be used to / get used to' is presented using crew biography-style sentences from a simulated personnel file. Helena matches each sentence to the correct structure and explains the temporal or habitual meaning. Practice (17 min): Helena completes a structured reading task — a 200-word simulated emergency procedure document containing 8 target grammar items (future perfect, future continuous, used to variations). She answers 6 comprehension questions, then identifies which grammar structure in the text each correct answer depends on. Production (35 min): Teacher delivers a full ASON-format simulation: one reading passage (300 words) about a vessel emergency scenario involving evacuation, distress call, and salvage — followed by 6 multiple-choice questions with a 12-minute timer. After submission, teacher and Helena debrief question by question, with Helena explaining her reasoning aloud for each answer. Teacher challenges any answer where Helena's reasoning was correct but insecure — building confidence in the justification, not just the answer. Wrap-up (10 min): Helena produces a 5-sentence oral summary of the simulated emergency scenario using at least 3 new vocabulary items and one future perfect structure. Teacher gives live feedback on accuracy and register.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — new): Future perfect (will have done) and future continuous (will be doing) as they appear in operational planning language and ASON exam texts — 'By the time the vessel reaches port, the crew will have completed all safety checks,' 'The harbor pilot will be boarding the vessel at 0600.' These structures appear in route plans, operational orders, and pre-departure documentation that ASON texts replicate. Also introduced: 'used to / be used to / get used to' as they appear in crew experience descriptions and adaptation narratives in ASON reading passages — 'The officer used to serve on tankers,' 'She is used to working night watches,' 'He had to get used to the new navigation system.' Exam skill: distinguishing future perfect from simple future in multiple-choice options where timing reference is the key comprehension lever. New vocabulary (10 words): evacuation (organized emergency exit from a vessel), life jacket (personal flotation device), life raft (inflatable emergency survival craft), fire suppression (system for extinguishing fires on board), watertight compartment (section of a hull sealed against flooding), emergency signal (distress communication — visual or acoustic), abandon ship (order to leave the vessel immediately), casualty (person injured or killed in a maritime incident), salvage (recovery of a damaged vessel or cargo), distress call (emergency radio communication — Mayday). Revision from Lessons 3 and 5 (3 words): distress, muster station, lifeboat drill. Collocations (new): transmit a distress call, activate a life raft, seal a watertight compartment, conduct an evacuation, coordinate a salvage operation. Expressions (new): man overboard (crew member has fallen into the sea), all hands on deck (everyone must report immediately), abandon ship (command form as an official maritime order), send out a Mayday (transmit an emergency distress signal).

tema: Precision Reading — Modal Perfects, Hedging Language, and the Language of Maritime Incident Reports
homework: Task 1 (25 min): Helena reads an authentic IMO Marine Accident Investigation report (teacher provides a 2-page excerpt from a real publicly available report via Google Drive — chosen for lexical accessibility at B2). She identifies and labels: (a) hedging language — minimum 5 instances; (b) advanced modals — minimum 3 instances; (c) 5 vocabulary items from today's lesson in context. She writes a 3-sentence summary of the investigation's main finding using her own words. Submission via shared Doc. Task 2 (10 min): Helena writes 5 sentences using today's advanced modals — one each for: would rather, had better, may as well, must have been, could have been — all set in a maritime incident context.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher shares two sentences on screen: 'The officer failed to maintain a proper lookout' (definitive) vs. 'It would appear that the officer may not have maintained a proper lookout' (hedged). Helena identifies which version would appear in a final investigation finding vs. an interim report, and why. Discussion surfaces the exam skill: ASON questions often ask what the text 'suggests' vs. what it 'states' — and hedging is the signal. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents advanced modals (would rather, had better, may as well) in maritime decision contexts — each example drawn from officer dialogue in a fictional incident report. Then hedging language is presented as a reading decoding tool — teacher shows a 5-sentence incident report paragraph with hedging highlighted, and explains how each hedge affects the strength of the claim. Helena categorizes each hedged sentence as: possibility / probability / uncertainty / recommendation. Practice (17 min): Helena reads a 220-word simulated formal investigation report (teacher-written in IMO register) and completes two tasks simultaneously: (1) underline all hedged language and modal structures; (2) answer 5 comprehension questions that test whether Helena can distinguish between 'the report concludes' and 'the report suggests.' Teacher reviews with screen annotation. Production (35 min): Full ASON simulation — one reading passage (310 words) built around a formal maritime investigation report, incorporating all grammar from Lessons 6 through 9 (cleft sentences, relative clauses, gerund-infinitive, future perfect, hedging, modal perfects). Helena answers 6 multiple-choice questions under a 13-minute timer. Debrief (15 min): Teacher and Helena map each question to the specific grammar or vocabulary lever — Helena names it before teacher confirms. This builds Helena's explicit distractor taxonomy across all Building and Expansion structures. Wrap-up (10 min): Helena defines 5 vocabulary items — negligence, root cause, finding, contributing factor, corrective action — in one connected paragraph describing a fictional incident.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — new): Advanced modals — 'would rather,' 'had better,' 'may as well' — as they appear in officer decision-making language and formal recommendations in ASON texts. 'The master would rather delay departure than risk navigating in reduced visibility.' 'The officer had better file the incident report before the port authority requests it.' 'Since the weather has deteriorated, we may as well wait for the pilot.' Hedging language (Expansion — new): passive recognition and comprehension focus — 'It seems that the deviation was caused by equipment failure,' 'It would appear that the crew was not adequately briefed,' 'To some extent, the incident could have been prevented,' 'More often than not, near misses go unreported.' ASON exam skill: hedging language in reading passages signals uncertainty or incomplete evidence — understanding hedged vs. definitive statements is critical for choosing between 'the text states' vs. 'the text implies' answer options. Integration of modal perfects from Lesson 2 (Foundation review): 'must have been,' 'could have been,' 'may have indicated' — now appearing inside hedged incident report language. New vocabulary (10 words): negligence (failure to exercise proper care), testimony (official statement given as evidence), investigation (formal inquiry into a maritime incident), finding (official conclusion of an investigation), recommendation (official suggestion arising from an investigation), contributing factor (element that helped cause an incident), root cause (primary underlying reason for an incident), corrective action (step taken to prevent recurrence), witness (person who observed an incident), sequence of events (chronological account of what happened). Revision from Lessons 5 and 8 (3 words): near miss, incident report, casualty. Collocations (new): conduct an investigation, identify the root cause, issue a recommendation, take corrective action, compile a sequence of events. Phrasal verbs (new): look into (an incident — recycled with new formal context), bring about (a corrective action), rule out (a contributing factor).

tema: Block 2 Full Simulation — ASON Exam Conditions, Structural Mastery Review, and Vocabulary Consolidation (End of Block 2)
homework: Task 1 (30 min): Helena completes a full ASON-format self-study reading set — teacher provides via Google Drive: 2 reading passages (authentic ASON 2025 or 2026 exam extracts, or teacher-reconstructed equivalents) with 6 multiple-choice questions each. Helena completes under timed conditions (25 minutes for both passages) with no assistance, marks her answers, then checks against the answer key provided. She writes a 5-sentence reflection in English: which question types were hardest, which grammar structure appeared most in the distractors, and what she will focus on in Block 3. Task 2 (15 min): Helena creates a personal vocabulary card set (physical or digital — her choice) for all 10 vocabulary items from today's lesson. Each card: front = word, back = definition in English + one example sentence in a maritime context. She photographs or exports the set and sends it to teacher as her Block 2 completion artifact.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher displays a one-slide visual summary of all grammar structures covered in Block 2 — each with one example sentence. Helena reads each example and names the structure. No correction yet — this is activation, not assessment. Teacher notes which structures Helena hesitates on — these receive targeted attention in the debrief. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents the subjunctive in 10 minutes using authentic ASON-register sentences drawn from ISM Code and STCW text. Helena compares: 'It is essential that the officer is present' (incorrect — common distractor) vs. 'It is essential that the officer be present' (correct — subjunctive base). Teacher shows 3 real exam-style answer sets where the subjunctive is the distractor mechanism. Remaining 8 minutes: rapid vocabulary presentation of today's 10 new words using a definitions-only slide (no translation) — teacher reads each definition, Helena produces the word. Practice (17 min): Helena completes a 12-item combined exercise — 6 grammar items (one each targeting: cleft, relative clause, gerund-infinitive, future perfect, hedging, subjunctive) and 6 vocabulary matching items from today's new words. This is a diagnostic review, not new learning — teacher grades live on screen and marks which structures remain insecure. Production (35 min): Full ASON Block 2 Final Simulation — exam conditions, zero assistance. Teacher shares 3 reading passages totaling approximately 650 words: Passage 1 — a port authority operational notice (200 words); Passage 2 — a formal vessel inspection report (230 words); Passage 3 — an excerpt from a maritime training manual (220 words). Helena answers 10 multiple-choice comprehension questions in 20 minutes (strict timer, no pausing). After submission, teacher conducts a full debrief (15 min): Helena reads each question aloud, states her answer, and explains her reasoning. Wrap-up (10 min): Helena reads the priority list aloud and articulates in her own words what she will watch for in each passage type. Teacher previews Block 3: navigation instruments, meteorology, and the language of watch-keeping — the vocabulary domain of the highest-difficulty ASON passages.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — new): Subjunctive basic forms as they appear in formal maritime recommendations and regulatory language — 'It is essential that the officer be present at the muster station,' 'The ISM Code requires that the master notify the port authority immediately,' 'It is recommended that all crew members complete the drill before departure.' ASON exam skill: the subjunctive base form (be, notify, complete — not be + -s, not past tense) appears in formal regulatory extracts and is a common distractor in answer options that offer 'is,' 'notifies,' or 'completed' as alternatives. Exam candidates who do not recognize the subjunctive select the distractor. Full grammar integration across Block 2 (review in application, not re-teaching): cleft sentences (Lesson 6), relative clauses with prepositions (Lesson 6), gerunds vs. infinitives with meaning shifts (Lesson 7), future perfect and future continuous (Lesson 8), used to / be used to / get used to (Lesson 8), advanced modals and hedging language (Lesson 9). Vocabulary consolidation — new (10 words): maritime authority (government body overseeing maritime safety and regulation), surveyor (official who inspects vessels for compliance), certificate (official document confirming a vessel or seafarer meets a standard), endorsement (official addition to a certificate confirming an extra qualification), port state control (inspection regime conducted by the port country on foreign vessels), deficiency (failure found during an official inspection), detention (official holding of a vessel due to safety failures), seafarer (professional who works aboard a ship — generic formal term), competency (proven ability to perform a required professional task), seaworthiness (condition of a vessel being safe and fit to sail). Revision across Blocks 1 and 2 (3 words): STCW, flag state, enforcement. Collocations (new): issue a certificate, conduct a port state control inspection, identify a deficiency, detain a vessel, demonstrate competency. Expressions (new): hold a valid certificate (have current official documentation), flag of convenience (vessel registered in a country for regulatory advantage), open registry (country that allows foreign vessel registration — context for flag state discussion in ASON texts).

tema: The Language of Maritime Contracts and Charter Agreements — Reading Dense Legal-Technical Texts at ASON Level
homework: Task 1 (20 min): Read the provided charter party extract (1 paragraph, shared via Google Docs) and underline every instance of past perfect or past perfect continuous. For each one, write one sentence in the margin explaining which event came first. Submit annotations directly in the document. Task 2 (15 min): Complete the 10-question vocabulary matching exercise (shared via Google Forms) — match each new word (charter party, demurrage, laytime, freight rate, shipowner, charterer, cargo claim, force majeure, arbitration, indemnity) to its definition in English. Target: 9/10 or above before next class.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Helena is shown two sentences on screen — one in simple past, one in past perfect — describing the same maritime event: 'The pilot boarded the vessel. The captain signed the departure log.' vs. 'The captain had already signed the departure log when the pilot boarded.' Teacher elicits what changes: not facts, but sequence and emphasis. Three more sentence pairs follow using vocabulary from Lessons 4–6 (clearance, stowage, manifest) to activate prior knowledge before the new grammar is presented. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents a simplified charter party dispute text on screen — a two-paragraph extract describing a cargo claim scenario where demurrage was applied because laytime had already expired when the discharge operation began. Past perfect and past perfect continuous are highlighted in yellow; simple past in blue. Helena reads the extract silently, then teacher elicits the temporal logic: which event came first? How does the grammar signal that? The 10 new vocabulary items are introduced through the text — no list drilling, only contextual unpacking. Each word is presented with its sentence context, a definition in English, and one exam-style question that tests comprehension of that word in a multiple-choice format. Practice (17 min): Helena receives a screen-shared gap-fill exercise — 8 sentences drawn from realistic charter party and cargo claim scenarios. Each gap requires choosing between simple past and past perfect. After individual completion, teacher reveals answers and debriefs two items where the distractor was simple past but the temporal logic required past perfect — exactly replicating ASON multiple-choice trap structure. Second activity: 5 sentences with missing collocations (file a ___, invoke ___, calculate ___) — Helena completes from memory, then checks against the text from Presentation. Production (35 min): Helena reads a full 250-word simulated ASON text about a charter dispute involving force majeure and a contested cargo claim. Four multiple-choice comprehension questions follow — two targeting vocabulary (demurrage, indemnity), one targeting past perfect sequence, one targeting a relative clause with a preposition at the end (recycled from Lesson 6). Helena works independently under timed conditions (12 minutes for reading + questions), then teacher debriefs each question: which answer Helena chose, what the distractor was designed to exploit, and what textual evidence confirms the correct answer. Debrief focuses on the process of elimination, not just the correct answer. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher recaps the past perfect rule in one sentence: 'Past perfect marks the earlier event when two past events are compared — and ASON uses simple past as the distractor.' Helena identifies which of the 10 new words she feels least certain about; teacher provides one additional sentence example for those words. Homework assigned.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — new): Past perfect and past perfect continuous as they appear in maritime incident narratives and contractual dispute language — 'The vessel had already departed when the amendment was issued,' 'The crew had been working double shifts before the malfunction occurred.' ASON exam skill: past perfect signals sequencing in incident reports and charter narratives — a primary distractor strategy is replacing past perfect with simple past in answer options to test whether the candidate tracks temporal logic. New vocabulary (10 words): charter party (contract between shipowner and cargo shipper), demurrage (penalty fee for exceeding agreed loading or unloading time), laytime (agreed time for loading or unloading operations), freight rate (cost charged for transporting cargo), shipowner (person or company that owns the vessel), charterer (party that hires the vessel), cargo claim (formal demand for compensation for damaged or lost cargo), force majeure (unforeseeable event that prevents contract fulfillment), arbitration (formal out-of-court dispute resolution), indemnity (compensation for loss or liability). Revision from Lessons 4 and 6 (3 words): bill of lading, liability, provision. Collocations (new): file a cargo claim, invoke force majeure, calculate demurrage, agree on freight rate, resolve through arbitration. Phrasal verbs in context: account for (delays), set out (terms of a contract), come under (a legal provision). Expressions (new): in the event of (if a particular situation occurs), subject to the terms of (governed by the contract), without prejudice to (recycled — consolidation in new contract context).

tema: Reading ASON Texts on Navigation and Meteorology — Precision Vocabulary and Conditional Logic in Technical Passages
homework: Task 1 (20 min): Read the provided meteorological incident report extract (shared via Google Docs — 200 words) and answer 5 multiple-choice comprehension questions independently, under timed conditions (10 minutes reading + answering, 10 minutes self-review). After completing, write one sentence for each wrong answer explaining why the correct option is better supported by the text. Submit via Google Docs. Task 2 (10 min): Write 3 original sentences — one third conditional and two mixed conditional — using at least 4 of the new meteorological vocabulary words. Sentences must describe a realistic maritime scenario. Submit via chat or Google Docs before next class.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher shares a screen with a simplified weather chart — isobars, a marked trough, and an arrow indicating vessel course. No labels. Helena describes what she sees using any English she has. Teacher introduces the meteorological terms as they become relevant to what Helena is pointing at — organic vocabulary entry through visual stimulus. Three conditional questions follow verbally: 'What would have happened if the captain had checked the barometric pressure?' 'If there had been a gale warning, what would the vessel have done?' This activates the third conditional before formal presentation. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents a 180-word simulated ASON incident analysis text — a vessel entered a trough without weather routing, a squall developed, and the incident report uses third conditional language throughout. The text is displayed on screen with third and mixed conditional clauses highlighted. Teacher works through the conditional logic: for each highlighted clause, teacher asks 'What was the real situation?' and 'What was the imagined alternative?' The 10 new meteorological vocabulary items are pulled from the text and presented in context, each with a one-sentence definition and one exam-style multiple-choice question testing word meaning in context. Practice (17 min): First activity — 6 conditional sentences with blanks where Helena must choose between third conditional and mixed conditional form. Sentences are set in maritime meteorological contexts using the new vocabulary. Second activity — 5 sentences where Helena identifies whether the conditional refers to a fully past scenario (third) or a past condition with present consequence (mixed). Teacher debriefs with emphasis on the ASON distractor pattern: 'would' without 'have' as the wrong answer in third conditional questions. Production (35 min): Helena reads a full 270-word ASON-format text about a vessel that failed to obtain a meteorological bulletin before departure, encountered a gale-force squall, and filed an incident report citing the absence of weather routing as a contributing factor. Five multiple-choice questions follow — two on vocabulary (meteorological bulletin, barometric pressure), one on conditional logic in the incident analysis, one on hedging language ('It would appear that...'), and one on a relative clause structure (recycled from Lesson 6). Helena works under timed conditions (13 minutes), then full debrief with teacher on answer elimination process. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher asks Helena to construct one third conditional sentence and one mixed conditional sentence using the day's new vocabulary — oral production, not written. This is not an exam skill, but it confirms active grammatical understanding. Teacher confirms which vocabulary items need additional exposure before Lesson 13.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Foundation — consolidation in new application context): Third conditional and mixed conditionals as they appear in maritime accident analysis and incident report language — 'If the officer had maintained the proper lookout, the collision would not have occurred,' 'If the vessel had been properly maintained, it would still be in service today' (mixed: past condition, present consequence). ASON exam skill: conditional logic in incident analysis is a high-frequency reading comprehension target — answer options frequently substitute 'would have' with 'would' or 'could' to create meaning-shift distractors. Third conditional was introduced in the Foundation sequence (Lessons 1–3 block) and is now applied with full maritime technical vocabulary for the first time. New vocabulary (10 words): weather routing (planned navigation path based on meteorological forecasts), isobar (line on a weather map connecting points of equal pressure), trough (elongated area of low atmospheric pressure), gale warning (official meteorological alert for strong winds), swell (long, rolling ocean waves generated by distant storms), current (steady directional flow of ocean water), tide (periodic rise and fall of sea level), barometric pressure (atmospheric pressure measured by a barometer), squall (sudden, sharp increase in wind speed), meteorological bulletin (official weather report issued for navigation). Revision from Lessons 2 and 3 (3 words): visibility, sound signal, waypoint. Collocations (new): issue a gale warning, monitor barometric pressure, adjust course for weather routing, navigate through a trough, transmit a meteorological bulletin. Expressions (new): stand into danger (navigate toward a hazard), heavy weather (severe sea and wind conditions), make for port (head toward a port, typically for safety), caught in a squall (suddenly encountered severe wind). Hedging language recycled in reading context: 'It would appear that the vessel failed to account for the trough,' 'It seems that no gale warning had been received prior to departure.'

tema: Ship Maintenance, Technical Inspections, and the Formal Register of Engineering Reports — Advanced Reading Strategies for ASON Texts
homework: Task 1 (25 min): Read the provided port state control report extract (300 words, shared via Google Docs) and answer 6 multiple-choice questions independently under timed conditions (15 minutes). For each question involving a modal perfect, write one sentence explaining why the correct modal was appropriate given the surrounding text. Submit annotations in the document. Task 2 (10 min): From the same text, identify all instances of dry dock, overhaul, corrosion, hull integrity, or propulsion system. For each one, write the full sentence in which it appears and a one-line definition in your own words in English. Submit via Google Docs.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher shares a screen with a port state control deficiency report — a real-format document (simplified) listing four deficiencies found on a vessel during inspection. Helena reads it silently for 90 seconds, then teacher asks: 'Which deficiencies are most serious? How do you know?' This activates vocabulary from Lesson 10 (deficiency, detention, seaworthiness, surveyor) and draws Helena into the technical register before new content is introduced. Teacher then asks: 'What should the crew have done before the inspection?' This naturally surfaces the modal perfect 'should have done' — which becomes the entry point for Presentation. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents a structured analysis of the four modal perfects on screen — a two-column table: left column shows the modal perfect form, right column shows its meaning in the context of a maritime engineering report. Four short example sentences from a realistic maintenance failure report illustrate each: 'The corrosion must have developed over several months' (logical deduction), 'The hydraulic system might have been compromised before departure' (past possibility), 'The crew should have conducted a dry dock overhaul the previous year' (unfulfilled obligation), 'The failure could have been avoided with proper lubrication' (unrealized possibility / indirect criticism). The 10 new vocabulary items are integrated into these example sentences and unpacked one by one. Teacher emphasizes the exam trap: all four modal perfects are grammatically possible — only the degree of certainty or type of judgment expressed in the surrounding text determines the correct answer. Practice (17 min): Helena receives a screen-shared exercise — 8 gap-fill sentences from maintenance and inspection contexts. For each gap, four modal perfect options are provided. Helena must select the correct one and write one word explaining her choice (certain / possible / obligation / criticism). Teacher debriefs each item, focusing on the two most commonly confused pairs: 'must have' vs. 'could have' (certainty vs. possibility) and 'should have' vs. 'might have' (obligation vs. speculation). Second activity: 4 sentences where Helena identifies which modal perfect was used and classifies its meaning — the same task format as ASON answer-option analysis. Production (35 min): Helena reads a 280-word simulated ASON text — a port state control inspection report on a vessel found to have hull integrity failures and a non-compliant propulsion system. The vessel was detained. Five multiple-choice questions follow: two on modal perfect meaning (which option correctly reflects the degree of certainty expressed in the report), two on vocabulary (overhaul, technical specification), and one on a cleft sentence structure (recycled: 'It was the hull integrity failure that led to detention'). Helena works under timed conditions (13 minutes), then full debrief. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher projects a single sentence on screen — 'The auxiliary machinery _____ been replaced before the inspection' — and asks Helena to complete it four different ways (must have / should have / might have / could have), explaining what each version communicates about the situation. This consolidates the lesson's core distinction in a low-pressure oral format. Homework assigned.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — new): Modal perfects in full productive and analytical range — 'should have done' (criticism or obligation not fulfilled), 'must have been' (logical deduction about the past), 'might have been' (possibility about the past), 'could have been' (unrealized past possibility or criticism) — as they appear in engineering incident reports, port state control findings, and maintenance failure analyses. ASON exam skill: modal perfect selection is one of the highest-frequency grammar traps in the exam — four answer options will use different modal perfects (must have / should have / might have / could have) with only one correctly matching the degree of certainty or obligation expressed in the text. Note: 'must have been' and 'could have been' were introduced in Lesson 2 as passive recognition; this lesson develops full analytical comprehension across all four modal perfect types. New vocabulary (10 words): dry dock (facility where a vessel is taken out of water for maintenance and repair), overhaul (comprehensive inspection and repair of machinery or structure), corrosion (deterioration of metal due to chemical reaction, typically rust), hull integrity (structural soundness of the vessel's outer shell), propulsion system (machinery that drives the vessel forward), auxiliary machinery (secondary onboard mechanical systems), wear and tear (gradual damage from normal use), lubrication (application of oil or grease to reduce friction in machinery), hydraulic system (system using pressurized fluid to operate mechanical components), technical specification (detailed description of required standards for equipment or systems). Revision from Lessons 4 and 10 (3 words): deficiency, seaworthiness, surveyor. Collocations (new): conduct a dry dock overhaul, assess hull integrity, identify corrosion, maintain a propulsion system, comply with technical specifications. Phrasal verbs in context: carry out (a full overhaul — third recycling in new technical context), look into (a propulsion failure), phase out (outdated auxiliary machinery). Expressions (new): out of service (not currently operational), fit for purpose (meeting the required standard), up to standard (compliant with specifications), sign off on (formally approve after inspection).

tema: Full ASON Reading Simulation — Multi-Text Exam Conditions with Strategic Comprehension Debrief (Mid-Block 3 Assessment)
homework: Task 1 (30 min): Re-read all three simulation texts from class. For each of the 10 questions, write a one-sentence justification for the correct answer using textual evidence — quote the specific words or phrase in the text that prove the answer is correct. Use the exam strategy expressions introduced in class (the text states that / according to the passage / the author implies that). Submit via Google Docs. Task 2 (15 min): From today's error analysis, identify the two question types where you made the most mistakes. Write a 3-sentence reflection in English: What made those questions difficult? What will you do differently in the next simulation? Submit via Google Docs or voice note — your choice.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher opens with one meta-question: 'In the ASON exam, what are the four types of multiple-choice questions you have encountered across the 2025 and 2026 papers?' Helena responds from memory — teacher fills gaps if needed, categorizing question types on screen: (1) vocabulary in context, (2) main idea or detail retrieval, (3) inference and implication, (4) grammar structure meaning. Teacher briefly explains that today's class is a full exam simulation and that the debrief is where the learning happens — the simulation itself is diagnostic. Full Simulation (45 min): Helena receives a three-text simulated ASON exam package — Text 1: a 200-word port state control inspection report (technical register, passive voice, modal perfects); Text 2: a 220-word COLREGS-based incident analysis (conditional logic, hedging language, inversion); Text 3: a 240-word charter party dispute extract (past perfect sequencing, cleft sentences, legal-technical vocabulary from Lesson 11). Ten multiple-choice questions distributed across the three texts, replicating the exact format and distribution of the 2025 and 2026 ASON English papers. Helena works in exam silence — teacher is present but does not intervene. Timer is visible. After 45 minutes, Helena submits answers via Google Form. Debrief (25 min — production phase): Teacher reveals answers one by one on screen. For each incorrect answer, teacher and Helena work through the elimination process together: What made the distractor attractive? What in the text confirms the correct answer? What grammar or vocabulary knowledge is the question testing? Teacher maps Helena's errors against the question type taxonomy established in Warm-up — is she stronger on explicit retrieval than inference? Stronger on vocabulary than grammar structure? This error pattern becomes the explicit planning input for Lessons 15 onward. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher summarizes error pattern in writing on screen — maximum three priority areas. Helena confirms whether this matches her own perception of difficulty. Homework assigned.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (integration — no new structure introduced): Full application of all grammar structures taught across Blocks 1, 2, and Lessons 11–13 in a simulated exam format. Grammar appears exclusively inside reading texts and answer options — not as taught content. Structures tested in context: passive voice and causative (Lesson 4), inversion (Lesson 5), cleft sentences and relative clauses (Lesson 6), gerunds vs. infinitives with meaning shifts (Lesson 7), future perfect and future continuous (Lesson 8), advanced modals and hedging language (Lesson 9), subjunctive (Lesson 10), past perfect (Lesson 11), third and mixed conditionals (Lesson 12), modal perfects — full range (Lesson 13). Vocabulary consolidation — new (10 words): passage (a navigated stretch of water or a section of a text — double meaning relevant to ASON), extract (a selected portion of a longer document), inference (a conclusion drawn from evidence not explicitly stated), implication (something suggested but not directly stated), paraphrase (restating an idea in different words — relevant to how ASON answer options reformulate text content), distractor (an incorrect answer option designed to mislead), stem (the question part of a multiple-choice item), option (each individual answer choice), explicitly stated (directly written in the text), implied (suggested but not directly written). Revision from Lessons 6, 9, and 10 (3 words): compliance, negligence, competency. Exam strategy expressions (new): the text states that (introduces explicit information), according to the passage (references text evidence), the author implies that (introduces inferred meaning), based on the context (explains vocabulary inference), the closest in meaning to (introduces paraphrase questions). tema: Inference, Implication, and the Language of Official Maritime Announcements — Targeting Helena's Identified Weak Points from Lesson 14
homework: Task 1 (20 min): Read the provided night orders extract (200 words, shared via Google Docs) and answer 5 inference-focused multiple-choice questions independently. For each question, identify whether the answer is explicitly stated or implied — write one sentence per question justifying your classification with a direct quote or paraphrase from the text. Submit via Google Docs. Task 2 (15 min): Write 4 original sentences using wish + past perfect — each one describing a realistic maritime situation involving regret or an unfulfilled obligation. Use at least 3 of the new vocabulary words from this lesson (standing orders, Navtex, watch schedule, roster, GMDSS, VHF). Submit via Google Docs or chat before next class.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher opens by displaying Helena's error map from Lesson 14 on screen — the two identified weak points (inference questions and grammar structure meaning, or whatever the actual error pattern revealed). Teacher states explicitly: 'Today we are targeting these two areas directly — through new vocabulary and a grammar structure that appears in the exact type of passage where you lost marks last week.' This connects the lesson to real exam evidence and positions the new content as a direct solution. Three warm-up sentences are displayed: 'The officer wished he had filed the report earlier.' 'The master wished the vessel were closer to port.' 'She wished the visibility had not deteriorated so quickly.' Helena reads them aloud and teacher asks: what do they have in common? What is the speaker feeling in each case? Teacher elicits 'regret' and 'desire for a different situation' before naming the structure. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents wish + past simple and wish + past perfect in a two-panel format on screen. Left panel: structure and meaning. Right panel: example sentences drawn from realistic ASON-style officer testimony and crew narratives. Teacher shows the distractor trap: a third conditional ('If the officer had filed the report, the detention would have been avoided') vs. a wish construction ('The officer wished he had filed the report') — same vocabulary, same past perfect form, but different meaning. Three exam-style questions test this distinction. The 10 new vocabulary items (circular, Notice to Mariners, port notice, Navtex, GMDSS, VHF, watch schedule, roster, standing orders, night orders) are presented through a realistic 150-word passage — a port notice distributed via Navtex instructing officers to monitor VHF channel 16 and comply with updated standing orders. Each item is contextualized before being defined. Practice (17 min): First activity — 6 sentences requiring Helena to choose between wish + past simple and wish + past perfect based on whether the situation is present or past. Second activity — 4 sentences where Helena must classify the answer choice in a mock ASON question: does this answer choice reflect what the text states (explicit) or what the text implies (inferred)? This directly addresses the inference weak point from Lesson 14 using the exam question type taxonomy established there. Teacher debriefs with emphasis on the linguistic signals that mark inference in ASON texts — hedging language (it would appear, it seems), absence of direct attribution, and paraphrase in answer options. Production (35 min): Helena reads a 260-word simulated ASON text — a passage combining a Navtex warning broadcast, a master's night orders, and a crew testimony extract where an officer expresses regret about not monitoring the VHF channel. Five multiple-choice questions: one on wish structure meaning, two on inference vs. explicit statement (the direct weak-point target), one on vocabulary (GMDSS, standing orders), and one on hedging language interpretation (recycled from Lesson 9). Helena works under timed conditions (12 minutes). Debrief focuses specifically on the inference questions — teacher shows Helena the exact words in the text that prove the answer is inferred rather than stated, and models the elimination process for paraphrase-based distractors. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher asks Helena to self-assess: 'Compared to last week's simulation, how did the inference questions feel today?' Teacher confirms which vocabulary items need reinforcement and previews Lesson 16. Homework assigned.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — new): Wish constructions — 'wish + past simple' (desire for a different present situation) and 'wish + past perfect' (regret about a past situation) — as they appear in formal narratives, crew testimony, and officer accounts within ASON reading texts. 'The master wished the vessel had undergone a full overhaul before departure' (past regret). 'The officer wished the gale warning had been issued earlier' (past regret — past perfect). These structures appear in testimony-style passages and narrative incident reports — a text type that appeared in the 2026 ASON paper. ASON exam skill: wish + past perfect is frequently confused with third conditional in answer options — recognizing that wish expresses desire or regret rather than cause-and-effect consequence is the key comprehension distinction.
