tema: The Language of Maritime Casualty Investigation — Reading Official Inquiry Reports and Causal Analysis Documents at ASON Examination Level
homework: Task 1 — Grammar precision writing (20 min): Helena writes 5 sentences in the style of a casualty investigation finding, each combining a modal perfect with a reported speech frame (e.g., 'The investigation concluded that the officer should have...,' 'The report indicated that the system must have...'). Each sentence must use a different modal perfect and a different reporting verb. Submitted as a typed document. Task 2 — Vocabulary application (15 min): Helena completes a 12-item matching exercise (Google Form provided by teacher) pairing each new term from Lesson 18 with its correct definition in investigation-report context — definitions are written in formal English, not glossed. Task 3 — Reading extension (20 min): Helena reads one page of a real IMO Marine Accident Investigation Report (teacher provides the specific URL in a shared document — a report with clear causal chain analysis). She highlights three sentences she finds most difficult to parse and annotates each with a brief explanation of the difficulty. Shared via Google Docs before Lesson 19.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up (10 min): Teacher displays on screen two sentences from a real-register casualty investigation summary — one using modal perfect inside reported speech ('The inquiry concluded that the officer should have maintained a proper lookout') and one using hedging inside a causal finding ('It would appear that the causal chain was initiated by inadequate bridge resource management'). Helena identifies: (a) the grammar structures layered in each sentence, (b) what degree of certainty each sentence encodes, (c) whether an ASON question on each would be 'the text states' or 'the text implies.' This activates all three integrated grammar skills before new vocabulary is introduced. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents the 10 new vocabulary items using a visual casualty investigation structure diagram shared on screen — the diagram shows the relationship between the causal chain, contributing factors, root cause, human error, systemic failure, and the formal outputs (collision report, grounding report, recommendations). Each new term is placed in its functional position in the diagram. Helena reads two sentences using each term in investigation-report register and provides a working definition before teacher confirms. Particular attention is given to 'voyage data recorder' and 'bridge resource management' — both have appeared in ASON texts and both are likely to appear as vocabulary-in-context questions. Practice (17 min): Helena receives a 400-word simulated flag state investigation report containing 8 instances of modal perfect + reported speech combinations and 5 instances of hedging language. She completes 3 targeted tasks: (1) underline all modal perfect + reported speech combinations and identify the certainty level of each; (2) circle all hedging signals; (3) answer 4 ASON-format comprehension questions — two explicit, two inferential — using the annotated text. Teacher debrief (7 min) focuses on the two inference questions and the hedging signals that determined the correct answer. Production (35 min): Helena receives a two-report reading set — a 300-word flag state investigation report and a 250-word coastal state investigation report covering the same incident from different institutional perspectives. She answers 10 ASON-format questions (8 single-text, 2 cross-text) in 30 minutes. The 5-minute debrief focuses exclusively on the 2 cross-text questions — where the flag state and coastal state reports attribute the causal chain differently — as this type of cross-text contradiction is a documented feature of recent ASON papers. Wrap-up (10 min): Helena adds today's error types to her running error log and identifies which of the two investigation registers (flag state or coastal state) produced more comprehension difficulty. Teacher records the finding for Lesson 20 planning.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — consolidation in new application context): Modal perfects in full analytical range ('should have done,' 'must have been,' 'might have been,' 'could have been' — Lesson 13) are now applied inside the specific text type of official casualty investigation reports, which represent the highest-density modal perfect environment in ASON reading material. New application layer: modal perfects appearing inside reported speech structures (Lesson 3) — 'The investigator reported that the propulsion system must have failed before the collision,' 'The inquiry concluded that the officer should have altered course earlier.' This combination of modal perfect + reported speech inside a formal investigation register is the most advanced grammar reading challenge Helena will face on the ASON exam. Grammar is not retaught; the lesson develops discrimination fluency in the most complex real-exam context. New vocabulary (10 words): marine casualty investigation (formal inquiry into a serious maritime accident conducted by a flag state or coastal state), flag state investigation (inquiry conducted by the country where the vessel is registered), coastal state investigation (inquiry conducted by the country in whose waters the incident occurred), collision report (official document recording the circumstances of an impact between vessels), grounding report (official document recording the circumstances of a vessel running aground), voyage data recorder (the maritime equivalent of an aircraft black box — records navigation data), bridge resource management (the practice of effectively using all available personnel and equipment on the bridge to ensure safe navigation), human error (mistake made by a person — as a formally categorized causal factor in investigation reports), systemic failure (a failure arising from inadequate procedures or organizational structures rather than individual error), causal chain (the sequence of events and decisions that collectively produced an incident). Revision from Lessons 9 and 5 (3 words): root cause, contributing factor, near miss. Collocations (new): conduct a marine casualty investigation, analyze the causal chain, retrieve data from the voyage data recorder, identify systemic failure, attribute human error as a contributing factor. Phrasal verbs in context: look into (a collision — sixth recycling, new investigative-inquiry frame), bring about (a systemic failure — recycled from Lesson 9 in new causal analysis context), rule out (human error as the primary cause — recycled from Lesson 9). Hedging language in investigation register (recycled from Lesson 9, new density): 'It would appear that bridge resource management was inadequate,' 'One could argue that the causal chain was initiated by the deviation from the approved route,' 'To some extent, the systemic failure may have been foreseeable.' Exam skill focus: official casualty investigation reports are the text type in ASON most likely to produce multiple inference questions in a single set — because investigation language is inherently hedged and probabilistic. This lesson trains Helena to move through hedging layers (the investigator said that it appeared that the officer may have failed to...) without losing track of what is stated vs. what is implied.

focoLinguistico: Grammar (Review — all structures from Lessons 1–19, no new structure introduced): This is the program's mid-point milestone lesson. All grammar structures taught across Blocks 1, 2, and 3 are consolidated through application in a full ASON-format simulation followed by a structured diagnostic review. Structures reviewed in application: modal perfects — must have been, could have been, may have indicated, should have done, might have been (Lessons 2 and 13); reported speech — all tenses (Lesson 3); passive voice and causative — have something done (Lesson 4); inversion for emphasis (Lesson 5); cleft sentences and relative clauses with prepositions (Lesson 6); gerunds vs. infinitives with meaning shifts (Lesson 7); future perfect and future continuous (Lesson 8); advanced modals — would rather, had better, may as well (Lesson 9); hedging language — full range (Lesson 9); subjunctive base form (Lesson 10); past perfect and past perfect continuous (Lesson 11); third conditional and mixed conditionals (Lesson 12); wish + past simple and wish + past perfect (Lesson 15). Results are scored, error-typed, and recorded as a formal mid-program baseline for comparison with the Lesson 38 final assessment.

tema: Advanced ASON Text Types — Reading Regulatory Circulars, IMO Resolutions, and Multi-Source Documents: End of Block 4 Consolidation
homework: Task 1 — Resolution parsing exercise (25 min): Helena reads one complete IMO resolution (teacher provides a short, accessible resolution from the IMO website — specific URL in the shared document). Task 2 — Vocabulary in sentence context (15 min): Helena writes 8 sentences using the new Lesson 20 vocabulary — one sentence per term, each in IMO resolution or regulatory circular register. Task 3 — Block 4 self-assessment (15 min): Helena reviews her error logs from Lessons 16–20 and writes a 100-word reflection (in English) on her single most significant comprehension improvement during Block 4 and her single most persistent challenge entering Block 5. Production (35 min): End-of-block ASON simulation — Helena receives a three-source reading set (total approximately 850 words): Source A is an IMO resolution operative section; Source B is an MSC circular implementing the same resolution; Source C is a flag state authority notice to operators about the implementation deadline and transitional provisions. She answers 12 ASON-format questions in 30 minutes: 4 from Source A alone, 4 from Source B alone, 4 requiring cross-source integration. After time is called, teacher conducts a full end-of-block debrief (15 min): Helena's Lesson 20 simulation score is compared against her Lesson 19 mid-program baseline, and the two results together are recorded as the Block 4 performance profile. focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — new application layer): Subjunctive base form (Lesson 10) and inversion for emphasis (Lesson 5) are now applied together inside the specific text type of IMO resolutions and maritime regulatory circulars — the most formally dense text type Helena will encounter on the ASON exam. These texts combine subjunctive in recommendations ('It is recommended that member states ensure,' 'The Assembly urges that flag states implement') with inversion in preamble clauses ('Noting that several flag states have failed to ratify,' 'Recognizing that the current framework does not adequately address') and cleft sentences in resolution operative paragraphs ('It is the responsibility of the flag state to enforce,' 'What the resolution requires is full implementation by all signatories'). No individual structure is retaught; the lesson trains Helena to navigate a single text that deploys all three simultaneously — the most advanced grammar reading demand in the program so far. New vocabulary (10 words): IMO resolution (a formal decision adopted by the IMO Assembly or Maritime Safety Committee), operative paragraph (the section of a resolution that sets out what is formally decided or required), preambular clause (the introductory section of a resolution that provides context and rationale), MSC circular (a formal communication issued by the Maritime Safety Committee to member states), MEPC (Marine Environment Protection Committee — IMO body responsible for environmental regulations), flag state obligation (a formal duty imposed on a vessel's country of registration by international convention), port state obligation (a formal duty imposed on a port country to inspect foreign vessels), implementation deadline (the date by which a regulation or amendment must be put into effect), transitional provision (a rule governing how an old and new regulation overlap during a changeover period), entry into force (the moment at which an international agreement or amendment becomes legally binding). Revision from Lessons 6 and 10 (3 words): convention, ratification, enforcement — the three terms most directly connected to IMO resolution language. Collocations (new): adopt a resolution, implement an operative paragraph, comply with a flag state obligation, meet an implementation deadline, trigger entry into force. Phrasal verbs in context: set out (resolution obligations — recycled from Lesson 6 in new IMO resolution register), come into force (entry into force — natural variant of 'entry into force' as phrasal structure), phase out (under a transitional provision — recycled from Lesson 4 in new regulatory context). Expressions in formal regulatory context (recycled): as set forth in (Lesson 6), without prejudice to (Lessons 6 and 11), by virtue of (Lesson 6) — all three now appearing in a single IMO resolution text, which is their natural habitat. Exam skill focus: IMO resolutions are among the most structurally intimidating texts in the ASON exam because their syntax is formal, recursive, and heavily nominalized. This lesson gives Helena a systematic method for parsing resolution language: (1) identify whether the sentence is preambular or operative; (2) locate the main verb; (3) identify what is being required, recommended, or noted; (4) apply the 'states vs. implies' distinction to the resolution's formal register.

tema: Environmental Compliance at Sea — Reading MARPOL Texts, Pollution Prevention Language, and MEPC Regulatory Documents in ASON Examination Conditions

Task 2 — Targeted re-reading (15 min): Helena re-reads the three texts from the Production stage without the questions, focusing exclusively on identifying every instance of discharge, non-compliance, and emission control area in context. She annotates in the shared document: for each instance, she writes one sentence explaining whether the term is being used in a prohibition, a description, or a finding. This trains the contextual precision that ASON questions on environmental texts exploit.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and lead-in (10 min): Helena is shown two short headlines — one about a vessel fined for illegal oil discharge, one about a fleet achieving ECA compliance ahead of the implementation deadline. Teacher asks: 'Based on what you already know from the program, which IMO body oversees these regulations? What document would the officer on watch need to maintain?' Helena reconstructs the regulatory chain (IMO — MEPC — MARPOL — Annex I — Oil Record Book) from memory, activating schema before encountering the text. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents the ten new vocabulary items using a MARPOL document structure diagram shared on screen — convention at the top, annexes below, then regulations, then appendices. Each new term is anchored to its position in the document hierarchy. Helena reads two short authentic-register extracts: one operative paragraph from MEPC.1/Circ.817 (MARPOL discharge prohibition language) and one PSC deficiency report citing failure to maintain an Oil Record Book. Teacher highlights used to / be used to / get used to inside a crew adaptation narrative embedded in the second extract and asks Helena to identify which form signals habitual past vs. present state. Practice (17 min): Helena completes a structured ASON-format task: four multiple-choice questions on the two extracts from Presentation. Questions are designed around the confirmed ASON 2026 distractor patterns — one question targets used to vs. be used to discrimination; one targets the subjunctive base form inside a MEPC recommendation; one targets the meaning of discharge as it appears in a prohibition clause (not 'dismiss' or 'complete' — common distractors); one tests whether the deficiency described falls under Annex I or general ISM non-conformity language. Teacher and Helena review each answer using the four-step resolution parsing method from Lesson 20: identify document layer, locate main verb, identify what is required, apply states vs. implies. Production (35 min): Helena works through a full ASON-format multi-text reading set of three documents — a MARPOL Annex I extract, an MEPC circular on ballast water management, and a PSC inspection report citing environmental deficiencies. Ten multiple-choice questions. Helena reads and answers under timed conditions (25 minutes), then the final 10 minutes are a structured debrief: teacher identifies which question types produced the most hesitation, maps each error to a specific vocabulary item or grammar structure, and records the pattern for Lesson 25 consolidation. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher introduces the collocation set for the lesson using a spoken sentence-completion drill — Helena completes the collocations orally with the correct preposition or noun: 'comply ___ MARPOL Annex I,' 'maintain ___ Oil Record Book,' 'operate within ___ emission control area.' Homework is assigned and confirmed.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — new application layer): Used to / be used to / get used to (introduced Lesson 8) applied inside environmental compliance narratives and officer adaptation accounts in MARPOL-register texts — 'Officers used to discharge ballast water without treatment,' 'The crew is used to following MARPOL Annex I procedures,' 'The fleet had to get used to the new emission control requirements.' Exam skill: distinguishing habitual past (used to) from present adaptation (be used to) from process of adaptation (get used to) when all three appear as answer options targeting the same sentence — a distractor pattern confirmed in ASON 2026 reading sets. Integration of subjunctive base form (Lesson 10) inside MEPC circular language: 'It is essential that the officer record all discharge operations in the Oil Record Book,' 'MARPOL requires that the vessel maintain an accurate Garbage Management Plan.' No structure retaught; application context is entirely new. New vocabulary (10 words): MARPOL (International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships — the principal IMO environmental framework), Annex I (the section of MARPOL regulating oil pollution from vessels), Oil Record Book (official log in which all oil-related operations must be recorded), ballast water (water taken into a vessel's tanks to maintain stability — regulated under the BWM Convention), emission control area (a designated sea zone where stricter limits on air pollution apply — also known as ECA), sewage (liquid waste generated onboard — regulated under MARPOL Annex IV), garbage management plan (official document describing how a vessel handles and disposes of waste), oily water separator (equipment used to remove oil from bilge water before discharge), discharge (the release of a substance from a vessel into the sea — regulated or prohibited depending on substance and zone), non-compliance (failure to meet a required environmental standard — with direct PSC and detention consequences). Revision from Lessons 6, 10, and 20 (3 words): MEPC, convention, enforcement. Collocations (new): comply with MARPOL Annex I, maintain an Oil Record Book, operate within an emission control area, process bilge water through an oily water separator, declare a garbage management plan. Phrasal verbs in context: phase out (older non-compliant equipment — seventh recycling, new environmental frame), carry out (an environmental inspection — eighth recycling), set out (MARPOL obligations — recycled from Lessons 6 and 20 in new environmental register). Hedging language in regulatory context (recycled from Lesson 9): 'It would appear that the discharge occurred within a restricted zone,' 'To some extent, the non-compliance may have been attributable to inadequate crew training.' Exam skill focus: MARPOL texts in ASON examinations are structured similarly to SOLAS texts but use a distinctive layered format — convention, annex, regulation, and appendix — each with different legal weight. This lesson trains Helena to identify which layer of the document a question is referencing before selecting an answer, since answer options frequently confuse annex-level obligations with convention-level principles.

tema: Flag State Obligations, Port State Authority, and the Language of Maritime Jurisdiction — Reading Multi-Layer Regulatory Texts Under ASON Examination Pressure
homework: Task 1 — Conditional reconstruction (20 min): Helena receives six sentences from the Lesson 22 Production texts that contain conditional logic. For each sentence, she rewrites it in a different conditional form (third to mixed, or mixed to third) and explains in one sentence how the meaning changes. She sends the six rewrites with explanations to the shared document before Lesson 23. Task 2 — Vocabulary in context reading (15 min): Helena reads one page of an authentic Paris MOU Annual Report (teacher will provide the specific extract via shared document). She identifies and highlights every instance of: risk profile, enforcement action, recognized organization, and flag state performance. For each highlighted term, she writes a one-sentence explanation of how it is being used — prohibition, description, finding, or recommendation. This task builds the noun-cluster precision that Lesson 22 assessment data showed as an emerging gap.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and lead-in (10 min): Teacher shares a simplified PSC detention order on screen — a real-format document with vessel name, flag state, port of inspection, deficiencies listed, and enforcement action stated. Helena reads for two minutes, then answers three oral comprehension questions: 'Which party issued this order?' 'What is the flag state's obligation in response?' 'If the deficiency had been rectified earlier, what would have happened?' The third question activates third conditional schema before the Presentation stage. Presentation (18 min): Teacher introduces the ten new vocabulary items in the context of the Paris MOU and Tokyo MOU frameworks — the two PSC regional agreements most referenced in ASON reading texts. A diagram on screen shows the relationship between IMO conventions, flag state obligations, recognized organizations, and port state authority. Helena maps each new term onto the diagram as it is introduced. Teacher then presents three sentences using cleft structures and conditional logic in authentic PSC-register language and asks Helena to identify: (1) which party is the grammatical subject; (2) whether the conditional refers to past, present, or hypothetical future; (3) what the consequence stated or implied is. Practice (17 min): Helena completes a structured gap-fill and classification task: eight sentences from authentic-register PSC and MOU documents, each with one answer option missing. Options target: conditional form discrimination (would have been vs. would be vs. will have been), cleft sentence subject identification, and vocabulary precision (recognized organization vs. classification society — not synonymous in PSC language). Teacher monitors and asks Helena to explain her reasoning for each choice before confirming, reinforcing the analytical habit the ASON exam requires. Production (35 min): Helena works through a full ASON-format reading set: two texts — a Paris MOU concentrated inspection campaign announcement and a flag state performance report. Ten multiple-choice questions, 25-minute timed reading. Questions include: three inference questions using hedging language, two conditional logic questions targeting mixed vs. third conditional discrimination, two vocabulary precision questions (MOU vs. convention, enforcement action vs. detention order), one cleft sentence attribution question, and two paraphrase recognition questions. Ten-minute debrief: teacher records error pattern by question type for Lesson 25 aggregation. Wrap-up (10 min): Oral consolidation — teacher reads six sentence stems aloud; Helena completes each with the correct collocation from the lesson set. 'The port state authority decided to _____ enforcement action.' 'The vessel's _____ profile indicated a high likelihood of deficiency.' 'The Paris MOU is a _____ of understanding between regional PSC authorities.' Homework assigned and confirmed.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — advanced integration): Third conditional and mixed conditionals (Lesson 12) applied inside jurisdictional dispute and flag state obligation language — 'If the flag state had enforced the STCW requirements, the officer would not have been serving without a valid certificate,' 'If the vessel had been registered under a stricter flag state, the deficiency would not have occurred' (past condition, past consequence); 'If the port state had detained the vessel, it would currently be undergoing overhaul' (past condition, present consequence — mixed). Exam skill: jurisdictional reasoning in ASON texts is frequently expressed through conditional logic — the candidate must track whether the condition refers to a past failure of the flag state, a present detention scenario, or a hypothetical future compliance outcome. Conditional confusion in this domain is a confirmed high-frequency error type. Integration of cleft sentences (Lesson 6) inside jurisdictional attribution language: 'It was the flag state that bore responsibility for the outstanding deficiency,' 'What the port state authority required was a valid statutory certificate.' No structure retaught; new application is in the specific domain of maritime jurisdiction, which Helena has encountered in fragments across Lessons 6, 10, 13, 16, and 20 but has not yet studied as a unified domain. New vocabulary (10 words): memorandum of understanding (a regional agreement between port state control authorities — as in the Paris MOU or Tokyo MOU), MOU (abbreviated form of memorandum of understanding — used in ASON texts referring to PSC regional regimes), concentrated inspection campaign (a coordinated PSC initiative targeting a specific safety issue across multiple ports and flag states), targeted vessel (a vessel selected for PSC inspection based on risk profiling), risk profile (an assessment of a vessel's likelihood of deficiency based on age, flag state, and inspection history), recognized organization (a classification society authorized to act on behalf of a flag state), flag state performance (the overall compliance record of a vessel's flag state — used in PSC risk targeting), enforcement action (a formal step taken by a port state or flag state in response to a deficiency or non-compliance), mutual recognition (the formal acceptance by one state of certificates issued by another), reciprocal obligation (a duty that applies symmetrically between two parties in a regulatory framework). Revision from Lessons 5, 10, and 16 (3 words): flag state, port state control, detention order. Collocations (new): conduct a concentrated inspection campaign, assess a vessel's risk profile, authorize a recognized organization, take enforcement action, invoke mutual recognition. Phrasal verbs in context: come under (PSC jurisdiction — ninth recycling, now in MOU regional frame), set out (reciprocal obligations — recycled from Lessons 6, 15, and 20), carry out (a targeted inspection — ninth recycling). Hedging language in jurisdictional context (recycled from Lesson 9, new density): 'It would appear that the flag state had failed to authorize the recognized organization prior to the inspection,' 'One could argue that the enforcement action was triggered by the vessel's risk profile rather than the specific deficiency.' Exam skill focus: ASON texts on PSC and flag state jurisdiction are among the most answer-option-dense in the exam — four options will each reference a different party (master, flag state, port state authority, classification society) as the responsible or authorized agent. Helena practices identifying the exact agent in jurisdictional sentences, including when responsibility is distributed across multiple parties in a single complex sentence.

tema: The Language of Maritime Personnel and Crew Welfare — Reading ILO MLC Texts, Duty Hours Regulations, and Seafarer Rights Documents at ASON Examination Level
homework: Task 1 — Register analysis writing (25 min): Helena receives three short paragraphs from the Lesson 23 Production texts — one regulatory, one descriptive, one testimony. For each paragraph, she writes two sentences: (1) one sentence identifying the register and explaining how she identified it (specific grammar structure, vocabulary item, or hedging pattern); (2) one sentence explaining how an ASON distractor might exploit a register confusion in a question about that paragraph. She sends the analysis to the shared document before Lesson 24. Task 2 — Vocabulary consolidation (10 min): Helena writes one sentence for each of the ten new vocabulary items from Lesson 23, placing each term in a context that is different from the Lesson 23 texts. Sentences must reflect MLC register — regulatory, not conversational. She sends these ten sentences in the same shared document as Task 1. This task ensures that the new vocabulary is encoded in productive memory rather than only in recognition memory — a consolidation step that supports the Block 5 final simulation in Lesson 25.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and lead-in (10 min): Teacher shares a short extract from an MLC inspection report on screen — three sentences describing a vessel where rest period records were found to be incomplete and a crew member had filed a grievance. Helena reads and answers two oral questions: 'What does the text state about the rest period records?' and 'What does the text imply about whether the seafarer was aware of the grievance procedure?' The second question requires an inference — activating the states vs. implies distinction from Lesson 14 in the new MLC register. Presentation (18 min): Teacher introduces the ten new vocabulary items using a visual map of MLC's five titles on screen — each title labeled with the terms it governs. Helena places each new term on the map as it is introduced, which builds the structural schema for reading MLC-based ASON texts. Teacher then presents two short authentic-register extracts: one from MLC Title II (hours of work and rest) and one from a seafarer employment agreement. Both extracts contain wish constructions and modal perfects. Teacher leads Helena through a guided annotation: for each modal perfect or wish construction, she identifies (1) whose perspective it reflects, (2) what time reference it encodes, and (3) whether it expresses regret, deduction, or possibility. Practice (17 min): Helena completes a structured ASON-format task: six multiple-choice questions on the two Presentation extracts. Question types: two register-discrimination questions (which answer option reflects regulatory language vs. testimony language), two vocabulary precision questions (repatriation vs. port welfare; grievance procedure vs. seafarer employment agreement), one wish + past perfect vs. third conditional discrimination question, one inference question requiring hedging language recognition. Helena explains her reasoning for each answer before confirmation — teacher records any reasoning gaps for the Lesson 25 debrief. Production (35 min): Helena works through a full ASON-format multi-text set: three documents — an MLC Title II extract on rest periods, a flag state inspection report citing MLC non-compliance, and a first-person crew testimony excerpt. Ten questions, 25-minute timed reading. Question design mirrors the three-register challenge described in the exam skill focus: questions require Helena to track which document contains the basis for each answer, a cross-text skill that ASON 2026 testing introduced at higher frequency. Ten-minute debrief: teacher aggregates the Lesson 23 error pattern with data from Lessons 21 and 22 to identify Helena's three most consistent error types across the block — this data drives the Lesson 25 consolidation design. Wrap-up (10 min): Collocation drill — teacher reads sentence stems; Helena completes orally with the correct MLC-register phrase. 'The flag state inspector found that the vessel had failed to _____ MLC rest period requirements.' 'The seafarer exercised her right to _____ a grievance under the seafarer employment agreement.' 'The shipowner is obligated to arrange _____ for any crew member who is stranded in a foreign port.' Homework assigned and confirmed.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — new application layer): Wish + past simple and wish + past perfect (Lesson 15) integrated with modal perfects (Lessons 2 and 13) inside crew welfare narratives and officer testimony extracts — 'The officer wished he had been allowed adequate rest before the watch,' 'The crew wished the MLC provisions had been enforced by the flag state.' Modal perfects embedded in the same testimony register: 'The rest period must have been shorter than the MLC minimum,' 'The duty roster could have been structured to comply with the regulation.' Exam skill: ASON texts on crew welfare frequently combine first-person testimony (wish constructions, modal perfects expressing regret or deduction) with third-person regulatory language (subjunctive, passive voice) in the same reading set. Helena must track which register — testimony or regulation — each answer option is reflecting, since distractors use testimony language to answer regulatory questions and vice versa. New vocabulary (10 words): MLC (Maritime Labour Convention — the ILO convention establishing minimum working and living standards for seafarers), rest period (the minimum continuous time off duty required under MLC regulations), hours of work (the maximum number of hours a seafarer may work in a given period — regulated under MLC), seafarer employment agreement (the formal contract between a seafarer and a shipowner — required under MLC), repatriation (the right and obligation to return a seafarer to their home country at the shipowner's expense), accommodation standard (the minimum requirement for crew living quarters on board), grievance procedure (the formal process through which a seafarer may raise a complaint under MLC), flag state inspector (the official authorized to inspect MLC compliance on vessels flying that flag's colors), port welfare (services and facilities available to seafarers in port — covered under MLC Title IV), manning scale (the minimum number of certified crew required by flag state authorities for safe vessel operation). Revision from Lessons 5, 8, and 10 (3 words): watchkeeping, seafarer, manning. Collocations (new): comply with MLC rest period requirements, file a grievance under the seafarer employment agreement, arrange repatriation for a crew member, inspect accommodation standards, verify the manning scale. Phrasal verbs in context: set out (seafarer rights — recycled from Lessons 6, 15, 20, and 22 in new ILO register), look into (a grievance — tenth recycling, now in crew welfare frame), phase out (non-compliant accommodation arrangements — recycled from Lessons 4, 7, and 21). Expressions in reading context (recycled in new semantic field): in accordance with (MLC Title II — recycled from Lesson 5 in crew welfare context), without prejudice to (seafarer rights under national law — recycled from Lessons 6 and 11), subject to the terms of (the seafarer employment agreement — recycled from Lesson 11). Hedging language in testimony register (recycled from Lesson 9): 'It would appear that the rest period had not been recorded accurately,' 'To some extent, the grievance procedure may not have been communicated to the crew.' Exam skill focus: MLC texts in ASON examinations require Helena to distinguish between what MLC mandates (objective regulatory language), what the ship did (factual description, often passive voice), and what the seafarer reported (testimony language, often hedged or modal-perfect-inflected). This three-register discrimination within a single text is among the most cognitively demanding reading tasks in the exam. This lesson builds systematic register-tracking as an explicit comprehension strategy.

tema: Cargo Claims, Limitation of Liability, and the Language of Maritime Insurance — Reading Highly Formal Legal-Commercial Texts at the Ceiling of ASON Difficulty
homework: Task 1 — Term-of-art annotation (20 min): Helena receives a 200-word extract from an authentic P and I Club circular (teacher provides via shared document). She reads the extract and identifies every multi-word noun phrase that functions as a legal or insurance term of art — terms that look like ordinary language but have a precise technical meaning in maritime law. For each term identified, she writes a one-sentence definition in English without using the term itself. This trains the disambiguation skill that the highest-difficulty ASON questions on legal-commercial texts require. Task 2 — Inversion transformation exercise (15 min): Helena receives eight sentences in standard declarative word order, all drawn from the maritime insurance and cargo claim domain. She rewrites each sentence using appropriate inversion — Not only..., Hardly..., Under no circumstances..., Never... — and then writes a one-sentence note on how the inversion changes the emphasis. She sends both tasks to the shared document before Lesson 25. These two tasks together consolidate the two highest-complexity grammar and vocabulary targets of Lesson 24 and ensure that Helena arrives at the Lesson 25 simulation with both structures in active analytical memory.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and lead-in (10 min): Teacher shares a single sentence from a P and I Club circular on screen: 'Not only has the shipowner failed to notify the Club of the deviation, but the letter of undertaking has, as a consequence, been suspended.' Helena reads once and answers three rapid oral questions: 'What two things are stated?' 'Which happened first?' 'Why does the inversion matter for how you understand the emphasis?' This activates both inversion recognition and sequencing logic simultaneously before the Presentation stage. Presentation (18 min): Teacher introduces the ten new vocabulary items using a maritime insurance claim lifecycle diagram — cargo loaded, damage discovered, surveyor engaged, claim filed, P and I Club contacted, letter of undertaking issued, limitation of liability invoked, arbitration or settlement. Each term is anchored to its stage in the lifecycle. Helena labels the diagram as terms are introduced. Teacher then presents two short authentic-register extracts: one from a general average notice and one from a limitation of liability clause. Both contain inversion and past perfect structures. Teacher leads Helena through a register-contrast analysis: 'This sentence uses inversion — what is being emphasized? Now read the paraphrase in option B — does the meaning shift or remain the same?' Practice (17 min): Helena completes a structured ASON-format task: six multiple-choice questions on the two Presentation extracts. Question types: two inversion-paraphrase equivalence questions (does the inverted sentence mean the same as the non-inverted option?), one past perfect sequencing question (which event occurred first?), two vocabulary precision questions (subrogation vs. indemnity; letter of undertaking vs. cargo insurance), one hedging language inference question. Helena explains reasoning for each answer before confirmation. Production (35 min): Helena works through a full ASON-format reading set: two documents — a P and I Club circular on cargo damage limitation procedures and a general average statement. Ten questions, 25-minute timed reading. This is the highest-density reading set in the program to date — teacher monitors pacing carefully and notes whether Helena maintains the slow, term-by-term reading strategy introduced in the Presentation. Ten-minute debrief: teacher highlights one confirmed error pattern from this lesson and connects it to the same error type if it appeared in Lesson 21, 22, or 23 — building the aggregated profile that drives Lesson 25 design. Wrap-up (10 min): Collocation drill — teacher reads sentence stems; Helena completes orally. 'The shipowner's P and I Club agreed to _____ a letter of undertaking to prevent vessel arrest.' 'The surveyor was engaged to _____ a report on the extent of cargo damage.' 'The carrier sought to _____ limitation of liability under the 1976 LLMC Convention.' Homework assigned and confirmed.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — advanced integration at program ceiling): Inversion for emphasis (Lesson 5) applied inside maritime insurance and limitation of liability language — the most formal written register Helena will encounter on the ASON exam. 'Not only did the shipowner fail to declare the full cargo value, but the insurer was also not notified of the deviation.' 'Hardly had the cargo been discharged when the cargo claim was filed.' 'Under no circumstances may the limitation of liability be waived by the carrier without express written consent.' Exam skill: inversion in insurance and legal-commercial texts signals a formal emphatic register that ASON answer options exploit by offering paraphrases without inversion — the candidate must recognize that the inverted original and the non-inverted paraphrase mean the same thing, or identify cases where the distractor subtly shifts the logical emphasis. Integration of past perfect and past perfect continuous (Lesson 11) inside cargo claim narrative language: 'The surveyor noted that the cargo had been improperly stowed before the vessel departed,' 'The crew had been loading in violation of the stowage plan for three hours when the shift supervisor intervened.' New vocabulary (10 words): P and I Club (Protection and Indemnity Club — the mutual insurance association that covers a shipowner's liability to third parties), hull and machinery insurance (insurance covering physical damage to the vessel's structure and propulsion systems), cargo insurance (insurance covering loss of or damage to goods being transported by sea), limitation of liability (the legal right of a shipowner to limit their financial exposure to a defined maximum — governed by the 1976 LLMC Convention), letter of undertaking (a written commitment by a P and I Club to pay a claim in lieu of arresting the vessel), vessel arrest (the legal detention of a vessel by a court order as security for a maritime claim), average (a system for sharing losses proportionally among parties to a maritime venture — general average or particular average), surveyor's report (the formal document produced by an independent marine surveyor assessing damage to cargo or hull), subrogation (the legal right of an insurer to pursue a claim on behalf of the insured after paying out), without prejudice (a formal legal designation indicating that a communication cannot be used as evidence in subsequent proceedings — recycled from Lessons 6 and 11 in its specific legal-insurance meaning). Revision from Lessons 11 and 14 (3 words): cargo claim, indemnity, bill of lading. Collocations (new): file a claim with the P and I Club, declare general average, issue a letter of undertaking, obtain a surveyor's report, invoke limitation of liability. Phrasal verbs in context: set out (the terms of the limitation of liability clause — recycled from Lessons 6, 15, 20, 22, and 23), account for (the full extent of the cargo damage — recycled from Lessons 4 and 11 in new insurance frame), rule out (subrogation as a recovery mechanism — recycled from Lessons 9 and 18). Hedging language in legal-commercial context (recycled from Lesson 9, highest density in the program): 'It would appear that the limitation of liability clause had not been invoked at the time the claim was filed,' 'One could argue that the surveyor's report does not sufficiently account for the pre-existing damage,' 'To some extent, the delay in issuing the letter of undertaking may have contributed to the vessel arrest.' Exam skill focus: maritime insurance and cargo claim texts represent the highest lexical density Helena will encounter in ASON reading material — every noun phrase is potentially a term of art (without prejudice, general average, letter of undertaking) that looks like ordinary language but carries a precise legal meaning. This lesson trains Helena to slow her reading speed on legal-commercial texts and treat each multi-word noun phrase as a potential term requiring definition before answering — the opposite reading strategy from the skimming approach appropriate for procedural or operational texts.

tema: Block 5 Consolidation and Targeted Error Correction — Full ASON Simulation Covering Environmental Compliance, Jurisdictional Language, Crew Welfare, and Maritime Insurance, with Individual Diagnostic Debrief
homework: Task 1 — Full simulation review (30 min): Helena re-reads both simulation text sets from Lesson 25 without the questions. For each text, she writes a three-sentence summary in English: sentence one states the main regulatory or operational topic; sentence two identifies the document type and its layer in the relevant regulatory framework (MARPOL Annex, MLC Title, MOU, P and I circular); sentence three identifies the register (regulatory, descriptive, or testimony) and names one specific linguistic feature that signals that register. She sends all four summaries to the shared document before Lesson 26. Task 2 — Targeted error correction (20 min): Helena receives from the teacher, via the shared document, the five questions from the Lesson 25 simulation that produced her most hesitation or error. For each question, she writes a one-paragraph explanation — not the correct answer, but the decision process: which strategy she should have applied, what the distractor was designed to exploit, and what the term or structure meant in context. This metacognitive writing task is the highest-value consolidation activity in the program for a candidate at Helena's level — it transforms passive error identification into an active correction protocol that she can apply independently in self-study sessions before the ASON exam.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and lead-in (10 min): Teacher displays a vocabulary timeline on screen showing all vocabulary introduced across Block 5 — organized by lesson and domain (environmental, jurisdictional, crew welfare, legal-commercial). Helena has two minutes to scan the timeline and identify, unprompted, any three terms she feels least confident about. She states them aloud with a one-sentence definition attempt for each. Teacher notes which terms Helena flagged vs. which terms the recorded error data flagged — any gap between Helena's self-assessment and objective error data is noted for the debrief. Presentation — pre-simulation strategy briefing (18 min): Teacher presents the Block 5 exam strategy framework — the five strategies listed in the focoLinguistico — as a structured one-page reference guide shared on screen. For each strategy, teacher shows a single example question from the Block 5 lessons where that strategy was the correct decision path, and a single example where a student who did not apply the strategy selected the distractor. Helena confirms her understanding of each strategy and identifies which one she found most difficult to apply consistently across Lessons 21–24. Practice — timed simulation (17 min): Helena completes Part 1 of the Block 5 consolidation simulation: two texts — a MARPOL Annex I extract and an MLC Title II inspection report — with ten multiple-choice questions. Strict timed conditions: 17 minutes, no teacher intervention, no dictionary. Teacher records pacing (which questions took longest) without interrupting. Production — extended timed simulation and debrief (35 min): Helena completes Part 2 of the simulation: two texts — a Paris MOU concentrated inspection campaign report and a P and I Club circular on cargo limitation and vessel arrest — with ten multiple-choice questions. Strict timed conditions: 25 minutes. After the timer, teacher and Helena work through all 20 questions together (10 minutes): teacher reveals the answer key, Helena self-scores, and for every incorrect or hesitated answer, teacher asks Helena to identify which of the five Block 5 strategies would have produced the correct answer — the goal is not to explain the answer but to train Helena to locate her own error type. Teacher then delivers the aggregated Block 5 diagnostic note verbally, walks Helena through her three most consistent error patterns with specific question examples from Lessons 21–25, and outlines the self-study protocol for before Lesson 26. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher closes the lesson by reading the Block 5 diagnostic note aloud — a one-paragraph summary of Helena's progress, naming the specific strengths confirmed (e.g., register-tracking, vocabulary precision in environmental and jurisdictional domains) and the two targeted areas for Block 6 (e.g., inversion-paraphrase equivalence in legal-commercial texts, hedging inference in multi-text cross-referencing questions). The note is saved to the shared document. Homework assigned and confirmed.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (consolidation — no new structure introduced): Full application of all grammar structures introduced or applied across Block 5 (Lessons 21–24) inside a timed ASON-format simulation: used to / be used to / get used to (Lesson 21 application layer), third conditional and mixed conditionals (Lesson 22 application layer), wish + past perfect with modal perfects (Lesson 23 integration), inversion for emphasis with past perfect and past perfect continuous (Lesson 24 integration). Grammar appears exclusively inside reading texts and answer options — not as taught content. Structures from all previous blocks also circulate in the simulation: subjunctive base form (Lesson 10), cleft sentences and relative clauses (Lesson 6), hedging language full range (Lesson 9), reported speech (Lesson 3), passive voice and causative (Lesson 4), modal perfects full range (Lessons 2 and 13). Vocabulary consolidation — Block 5 cumulative review (10 words drawn from high-error vocabulary across Lessons 21–24, selected based on Helena's recorded error pattern from Lessons 21–24 debriefs): The specific ten words are confirmed by the teacher from the aggregated error data before Lesson 25 begins. Default set if error data is insufficient to override: MARPOL, Oil Record Book, memorandum of understanding, rest period, grievance procedure, P and I Club, limitation of liability, letter of undertaking, concentrated inspection campaign, recognized organization — the ten terms most frequently involved in distractor confusion across Block 5 texts. Revision from full program arc (3 words): causal chain, compliance, flag state — the three terms that connect the environmental, jurisdictional, crew welfare, and insurance domains covered in Block 5. Exam strategy consolidation for Block 5: (1) document-layer identification before answering (MARPOL Annex vs. convention level; MLC Title vs. general MLC obligation; P and I circular vs. LLMC statutory text); (2) register-tracking across multi-text sets (regulatory vs. descriptive vs. testimony); (3) term-of-art disambiguation in legal-commercial texts; (4) inversion paraphrase equivalence testing; (5) hedging language inference discrimination — the text states vs. the text implies. Block 5 error profile synthesis: teacher aggregates the recorded error types from Lessons 21, 22, 23, and 24 into a written diagnostic note shared with Helena at the end of Lesson 25 — this note names Helena's three most consistent error patterns, maps each to a specific text type and question format, and prescribes the targeted homework and self-study protocol for Block 6. This diagnostic note becomes the input for Block 6 lesson design.

tema: Admiralty Charts, Route Planning Documents, and the Language of Navigational Authority — Reading SOLAS Chapter V Texts at ASON Examination Level
homework: Task 1 — Vocabulary consolidation (20 min): Helena writes one sentence for each of the ten new vocabulary items introduced in Lesson 26, using each word in a context drawn from SOLAS Chapter V navigational requirements. Sentences must be in the register of a formal navigational report (third person, passive voice where appropriate, no contractions). Helena sends the ten sentences as a shared document before Lesson 27. focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — advanced integration, no new structure introduced): All structures already taught are applied simultaneously inside the specific text type of SOLAS Chapter V navigational safety requirements — the chapter most directly relevant to Helena's target role as a Ship's Pilot and the most frequently cited SOLAS source in ASON reading sets. Grammar emphasis this lesson: cleft sentences and relative clauses with prepositions (Lesson 6) embedded inside navigational authority language ('It is the master who bears ultimate responsibility for the safety of navigation,' 'The chart to which the officer referred had not been updated'); subjunctive base form (Lesson 10) in SOLAS recommendations ('It is required that the officer on watch maintain a continuous lookout'); modal perfects (Lessons 2 and 13) in navigational failure analysis ('The chart should have been updated before departure,' 'The officer must have been relying on an outdated edition'). Exam skill: SOLAS Chapter V texts combine dense nominalization with embedded relative clauses and subjunctive obligations — a structural profile confirmed in both ASON 2025 and 2026 reading sets. No structure is retaught; the lesson develops simultaneous multi-structure discrimination inside a single authoritative document type. New vocabulary (10 words): nautical chart (an official navigational map produced to a specific scale showing depths, hazards, and aids to navigation), chart datum (the reference level used as the baseline for depth measurements on a nautical chart), Notice to Mariners update (a specific correction issued to bring a nautical chart into conformity with current conditions — distinct from the general Notice to Mariners circular already taught in Lesson 15), electronic chart display (the digital navigation system displaying chart data in real time — formally known as ECDIS), paper chart (a printed nautical chart carried as a backup or primary navigation tool depending on vessel class), aids to navigation (fixed or floating objects such as buoys and lighthouses that assist in determining position), traffic lane (a designated directional channel within a traffic separation scheme — more specific than the TSS term already taught), pilot station (the designated location where a harbor pilot boards or disembarks a vessel), compulsory pilotage (the legal requirement for a vessel to take on a licensed pilot in certain waters), underkeel clearance (the minimum required distance between the vessel's keel and the seabed). Revision from Lessons 2, 3, and 12 (3 words): waypoint, traffic separation scheme, weather routing. Collocations (new): update a nautical chart, verify underkeel clearance, comply with compulsory pilotage requirements, display an electronic chart, identify aids to navigation. Phrasal verbs in context: set out (navigational requirements — tenth recycling, now in SOLAS Chapter V frame), come under (compulsory pilotage jurisdiction — recycled from Lessons 6, 16, 22, and 25), carry out (a chart update verification — tenth recycling). Hedging language in navigational authority context (recycled from Lesson 9, applied to SOLAS register): 'It would appear that the electronic chart had not been updated to the current edition,' 'To some extent, the failure to verify underkeel clearance may have contributed to the grounding.' Exam skill focus: SOLAS Chapter V is among the three most-cited primary sources in ASON reading passages because it governs navigational safety — Helena's target professional domain. This lesson trains Helena to read SOLAS extracts using the four-step resolution parsing method introduced in Lesson 20 (identify preambular vs. operative; locate main verb; identify what is required; apply the states-vs.-implies distinction) now adapted for SOLAS chapter structure, which uses Regulation numbers rather than preambular and operative paragraphs. The lesson also addresses the specific ASON distractor pattern in which one answer option correctly identifies the SOLAS obligation but attributes it to the wrong party (officer vs. master vs. flag state vs. port state).

tema: The Language of Vessel Traffic Services and Port Approach Communication — Reading VTS Procedures, Pilot Boarding Protocols, and Port Entry Regulations in ASON Multi-Text Sets
homework: Task 1 — Register-tracking annotation (20 min): Helena takes the two-text simulation set from the Production stage of Lesson 27 and completes a written register analysis for each answer option she got wrong or was uncertain about. Helena sends the audio recording before Lesson 28.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and Lead-in (10 min): Teacher displays on shared screen a simplified diagram of a port approach zone showing the VTS monitoring area, mandatory reporting points, pilot station, fairway, and berth. Text A: a port authority notice setting out the conditions for port entry, including mandatory reporting requirements and tide window constraints. Text B: a VTS communication log in which a vessel fails to meet two of the conditions and the VTS operator issues a formal advisory. Six questions span both texts and include: two party-identification questions (who is responsible for what under each document), two modal perfect questions in the debrief following a near-miss described in Text B, one vocabulary inference question on 'tide window,' and one register-discrimination question ('Which of the following is stated in the VTS procedure document rather than implied by the communication log?').
