focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — advanced integration, no new structure introduced): Reported speech (Lesson 3) integrated with future perfect and future continuous (Lesson 8) inside VTS communication logs and port approach operational documents — the text type in which these two structures co-occur most naturally in real maritime documentation. 'The VTS operator reported that the vessel would be entering the restricted zone at 0400,' 'The harbor master indicated that the pilot would have boarded the vessel before it reached the waypoint.' Exam skill: ASON texts based on VTS communication logs require Helena to track temporal sequencing across reported speech backshifts and future perfect time references simultaneously — a grammar discrimination task confirmed as a high-frequency error pattern in Block 5. Integration of gerunds vs. infinitives with meaning shifts (Lesson 7) in VTS instruction language: 'The operator reminded the master to check the underkeel clearance' (obligation) vs. 'The operator remembered checking the VHF channel' (past recall) — distractor pairs of this type appear in ASON answer options targeting VTS procedure descriptions. No structure retaught; application context is entirely new. New vocabulary (10 words): Vessel Traffic Service (a shore-based authority that monitors and regulates vessel movement in a defined port approach or restricted waterway), VTS operator (the qualified shore-based officer responsible for monitoring and communicating with vessels in a VTS zone), traffic image (the VTS operator's complete real-time picture of all vessels in the monitored zone), mandatory reporting point (a defined geographic position at which a vessel is required to contact VTS and report its position and intentions), port approach (the navigational route a vessel follows from open sea to the point of pilot boarding), vessel movement plan (a pre-submitted schedule of a vessel's intended arrival, movements, and departure within a port), port entry permit (formal authorization issued by a port authority allowing a vessel to enter port waters), berthing assignment (the specific berth allocated to a vessel by the port authority for a given call), fairway (the navigable channel within a port or harbor used for vessel transit), tide window (the limited period during which tidal conditions are sufficient to permit safe passage of a vessel with deep draft). Revision from Lessons 2, 15, and 26 (3 words): pilot station, compulsory pilotage, VHF. Collocations (new): obtain a port entry permit, submit a vessel movement plan, report at a mandatory reporting point, navigate within the fairway, exploit the tide window. Phrasal verbs in context: come under (VTS authority — recycled from Lessons 6, 16, 22, 25, and 26), set out (port entry conditions — eleventh recycling in new port authority frame), carry out (a vessel movement plan — eleventh recycling). Hedging language in VTS communication context (recycled from Lesson 9): 'It would appear that the vessel failed to report at the mandatory reporting point,' 'It seems that the port entry permit had not been obtained prior to the vessel's arrival at the fairway entrance.' Exam skill focus: VTS procedure texts represent a high-frequency ASON text type in which the same information is presented in two registers within the same multi-text set — a formal VTS procedure document (regulatory, subjunctive, passive voice) and a VTS communication log (reported speech, past tense, hedged). Helena practices identifying which register each answer option is drawn from, since distractors frequently quote testimony language to answer a question about regulatory obligation, or vice versa. This is the register-tracking skill introduced systematically in Lesson 23 and now applied inside the port approach operational domain most relevant to Helena's target role as a harbor pilot.

tema: Collision Regulations in Practice — Reading COLREGS Rule Applications, Court Findings, and Technical Expert Reports at the Ceiling of ASON Complexity
homework: Task 1 — Three-register annotation (25 min): Helena takes the three-text simulation from Lesson 28 and produces a written annotation for each paragraph identifying: (a) text type (COLREGS rule / investigation report / expert opinion); (b) the dominant grammar structure in that paragraph (subjunctive / modal perfect / inversion / cleft sentence / hedging / reported speech); (c) any vocabulary item from the Lesson 28 set that appears in that paragraph. Helena sends the annotated document before Lesson 29. Task 2 — Cross-text question writing (15 min): Helena writes two original ASON-format multiple-choice questions based on the three-text simulation set. Each question must require evidence from two different texts to answer correctly. For each question, Helena also writes an explanation of why each of the four answer options is correct or incorrect and which text type the distractor options are drawn from. This reverse-engineering task builds Helena's awareness of how ASON question writers exploit register and party-attribution confusion. Task 3 — Vocabulary self-testing (10 min): Without referring to notes, Helena writes a one-sentence definition in English for each of the ten new vocabulary items from Lesson 28, then checks against the Lesson 28 vocabulary definitions. She identifies any item whose definition she could not produce accurately and marks it for priority revision in Lesson 29.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and Lead-in (10 min): Teacher presents a simple radar-plot diagram on shared screen showing two vessels in a crossing situation, with bearing lines and PCA data. Without any text, teacher asks Helena to narrate what COLREGS obligation each vessel has, using vocabulary from Lessons 3, 12, and today's new set. Helena identifies the give-way and stand-on vessels, names the applicable rule (Rule 15), and describes what each vessel should have done using modal perfects. This activates the grammar-vocabulary intersection before the text work begins. Teacher introduces the three-text format: Helena will work with a COLREGS extract, a collision investigation report, and a technical expert opinion — three registers, one incident. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents the ten new vocabulary items in three groups anchored to the three text types. Group 1 (COLREGS rule application: rule application, crossing situation, overtaking situation, head-on situation, risk of collision) — each term introduced through the relevant COLREGS rule number and a formal definition. Teacher highlights the subjunctive and passive voice constructions through which these terms appear in the rules themselves. Group 2 (investigation vocabulary: early and substantial action, point of closest approach, action of last resort, post-collision statement) — introduced through a short investigation report extract. Group 3 (legal vocabulary: court of inquiry finding) — introduced through a one-sentence expert opinion extract. Teacher models the register shift between the three groups explicitly. Practice (17 min): Teacher presents four targeted ASON-format questions — one per text type plus one cross-text question. Question 1 (COLREGS extract): subjunctive in Rule 16 — 'It is required that the give-way vessel take early and substantial action' — distractor offers 'takes' in indicative. Question 2 (investigation report): modal perfect attribution — 'The officer should have altered course at the first point of observation' — distractor substitutes 'must have altered.' Question 3 (expert opinion): inversion paraphrase — 'Not only did the give-way vessel fail to alter course, but it also failed to sound the appropriate signal' — distractor offers a non-inverted paraphrase with shifted emphasis. Question 4 (cross-text): party attribution — answer requires identifying which text establishes the obligation and which text identifies the failure. Helena answers independently, teacher debriefs with full error-type analysis. Production (35 min): Full three-text ASON simulation. Text A: COLREGS Rules 13, 14, and 15 extracts. Text B: A collision investigation report on a crossing situation in a port approach channel. Text C: A technical expert opinion excerpt analyzing whether early and substantial action was taken. Seven questions span all three texts, including two cross-text questions and one question requiring Helena to identify the text type from which an answer option is drawn. Helena completes the simulation under timed conditions (28 minutes). Debrief (7 minutes): teacher reconstructs the two most difficult questions using the four-step parsing method and register-tracking protocol. Wrap-up (10 min): Helena identifies how each of the three revision vocabulary items (give-way vessel, stand-on vessel, causal chain) appeared across the three texts in different registers and confirms the grammatical form in which each appeared.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — advanced integration, no new structure introduced): The full grammar architecture accumulated across the program is applied inside the most complex text type Helena will encounter in ASON — a three-text set combining: (1) a COLREGS rule extract (subjunctive, passive voice, formal register); (2) a collision investigation report (modal perfects, reported speech, past perfect, hedging language); (3) a technical expert opinion (inversion for emphasis, cleft sentences, conditional logic). This three-register combination within a single examination set has appeared in both the ASON 2025 and 2026 papers and represents the ceiling-level comprehension demand. Grammar emphasis this lesson: inversion for emphasis (Lesson 5) inside expert opinion language — 'Not only did the stand-on vessel fail to maintain course and speed, but the give-way vessel had also ignored the sound signal'; modal perfects inside investigation findings embedded in reported speech — 'The court found that the officer should have altered course no later than the point of closest approach'; cleft sentences in legal attribution — 'It was the failure to maintain a proper lookout that was identified as the primary cause.' All structures appear simultaneously across three text types without any single structure being retaught. Exam skill: the three-text ASON set is the highest-demand format because questions may draw evidence from any of the three texts, and answer options may reproduce language from the wrong text type to create register and party-attribution distractors. New vocabulary (10 words): rule application (the process of determining which COLREGS rule governs a specific encounter situation between two vessels), crossing situation (a scenario in which two vessels approach each other at an angle creating a risk of collision, governed by COLREGS Rule 15), overtaking situation (a scenario in which one vessel approaches another from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the beam, governed by COLREGS Rule 13), head-on situation (a scenario in which two power-driven vessels approach each other on reciprocal courses, governed by COLREGS Rule 14), risk of collision (the condition that triggers the obligation to take avoiding action under COLREGS — determined by compass bearing), early and substantial action (the requirement under COLREGS Rule 16 that avoiding action be taken in time to be obvious to the other vessel), point of closest approach (the moment in a vessel's trajectory at which it will be nearest to another vessel — abbreviated PCA in investigation reports), action of last resort (emergency maneuver taken when collision is imminent despite all earlier actions, governed by COLREGS Rule 17), post-collision statement (a formal written account of events produced by the master or officer following an impact — used in casualty investigation proceedings), court of inquiry finding (an officially recorded conclusion produced by a maritime court or formal investigation panel). Revision from Lessons 3, 9, and 18 (3 words): give-way vessel, stand-on vessel, causal chain. Collocations (new): determine the risk of collision, take early and substantial action, calculate the point of closest approach, produce a post-collision statement, apply COLREGS Rule 15. Phrasal verbs in context: carry out (Rule application analysis — twelfth recycling), rule out (action of last resort as a factor — recycled from Lessons 9, 18, and 24), account for (the crossing situation geometry — recycled from Lessons 4, 11, and 24 in new navigational frame). Hedging language in expert opinion register (recycled from Lesson 9, maximum density): 'One could argue that the give-way vessel's failure to take early and substantial action initiated the causal chain,' 'To some extent, the stand-on vessel's action of last resort may have contributed to the severity of the impact,' 'It would appear that neither vessel had accurately assessed the risk of collision at the first point of observation.' Exam skill focus: COLREGS-based ASON questions are the grammar-densest question type because the rules themselves use formal imperative and subjunctive constructions, investigation reports apply modal perfects to the same events, and expert opinions use inversion and cleft sentences to assign legal attribution. Helena's error profile from Block 5 (shared by teacher before this lesson) is likely to include modal perfect confusion in Rule-application contexts and party-attribution errors in three-text sets — this lesson directly targets both patterns at maximum program complexity.

tema: Cargo Documentation, Seaworthiness Obligations, and the Language of Shipowner Liability — Reading Complex Multi-Party Legal-Operational Texts at Full ASON Examination Density
homework: Task 1 — Conditional and sequencing analysis (20 min): Helena takes the three-text simulation from Lesson 29 and identifies every instance of past perfect, past perfect continuous, third conditional, or mixed conditional in all three texts. For each instance, she writes: (a) the grammar structure; (b) what temporal or hypothetical relationship it establishes; (c) which party's position or obligation it modifies. Helena sends this analysis before Lesson 30. Task 2 — Term-of-art disambiguation practice (15 min): Helena reviews the ten new vocabulary items from Lesson 29 alongside the ten from Lesson 24 (P and I Club, hull and machinery insurance, cargo insurance, limitation of liability, letter of undertaking, vessel arrest, average, surveyor's report, subrogation, without prejudice) and creates a written two-column comparison for any pair of terms that could be confused in an ASON answer option. For each pair, she writes one sentence showing how the two terms differ in a single liability scenario. This produces a personal disambiguation reference document that Helena brings to Lesson 30. Task 3 — Synthesis reading (15 min): Helena reads the IMO's publicly available summary of the Hague-Visby Rules framework (accessible through imo.org or through the IMO's legal instruments database) and identifies two sentences in the source text that directly correspond to vocabulary items from Lesson 29. She copies the sentences, identifies the vocabulary items, and annotates the grammar structure used in each sentence. Helena sends the annotated sentences with the other homework before Lesson 30.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and Lead-in (10 min): Teacher opens a shared document showing a simplified bill of lading with fictional vessel and cargo details. Teacher asks Helena to identify what the document establishes — who the parties are, what the cargo is, and what obligations are implied — using vocabulary from Lessons 4, 11, 24, and today's set. Helena narrates a spoken summary in three sentences, each targeting a different party's obligation. Teacher introduces the lesson focus: today's texts concern what happens when those obligations are not met — cargo claims, seaworthiness failures, and the legal language through which liability is established and contested. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents the ten new vocabulary items in two groups. Group 1 (liability framework vocabulary: seaworthiness obligation, cargo worthiness, inherent vice, deviation from voyage, general average contribution) — each term introduced through a one-sentence ASON-register definition on screen, followed by a formal legal sentence in which the term appears, with grammar structure highlighted. Group 2 (documentation and procedure vocabulary: Hague-Visby Rules, carrier liability limit, cargo survey, letter of protest, sea protest) — introduced through a short cargo claim correspondence extract on screen. Teacher connects each new term to vocabulary already known (seaworthiness from Lesson 10, cargo claim from Lesson 11, general average from Lesson 24, surveyor's report from Lesson 24) to reinforce the accumulation pattern and prevent the learning-as-new error. Practice (17 min): Teacher presents four targeted ASON-format questions based on a two-text set — Text A is a Hague-Visby Rules extract on the seaworthiness obligation; Text B is a cargo claim correspondence including a letter of protest and a cargo survey reference. Question 1 targets past perfect sequencing: 'The cargo had already been loaded when the survey was conducted' — distractor substitutes simple past. Question 2 targets third conditional logic in liability analysis: 'If the seaworthiness obligation had been fulfilled, the general average contribution would not have been declared' — distractor substitutes mixed conditional. Question 3 targets term-of-art disambiguation: 'inherent vice' vs. 'deviation from voyage' as the applicable defense. Question 4 targets document-layer identification: Helena must identify whether the statement reflects the Hague-Visby Rules standard or the bill of lading contract. Helena answers independently, teacher debriefs with full error-type labeling. Production (35 min): Three-text ASON simulation. Text A: a Hague-Visby Rules liability framework extract. Text B: a cargo survey report. Text C: a letter of protest issued by the master. Seven questions span all three texts, including two cross-text questions, two modal perfect questions in the context of a cargo damage analysis, and one vocabulary inference question on 'inherent vice.' Helena completes the simulation under timed conditions (28 minutes). Debrief (7 minutes): teacher focuses on the two cross-text questions and the inherent vice inference question, reconstructing each using the three-layer document discrimination strategy. Wrap-up (10 min): Helena completes a spoken round — for each of the three revision vocabulary items (bill of lading, cargo claim, subrogation), she places it in the correct document layer (bill of lading contract / Hague-Visby Rules / insurance recovery mechanism) and gives one sentence explaining the party who invokes or relies on it.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (Expansion — advanced integration, consolidation at full program density): Past perfect and past perfect continuous (Lesson 11) integrated with third conditional and mixed conditional logic (Lesson 12) inside shipowner liability and cargo documentation texts — the co-occurrence pattern most frequently exploited in ASON answer options targeting the highest-difficulty questions in the exam. 'The cargo had been loaded in violation of the stowage plan before the vessel departed' (past perfect sequencing); 'The crew had been operating with a known hydraulic fault for six hours when the master was informed' (past perfect continuous duration); 'If the seaworthiness obligation had been met, the cargo damage would not have occurred' (third conditional); 'If the vessel had been properly classed, it would currently hold a valid statutory certificate' (mixed conditional: past condition, present consequence). Exam skill: the highest-difficulty ASON questions combine temporal sequencing (past perfect), hypothetical analysis (conditional), and party attribution (cleft sentences or inversion) in a single answer option — Helena must track all three simultaneously to discriminate between near-identical options. Integration of inversion (Lesson 5) and cleft sentences (Lesson 6) inside legal attribution language: 'It was the shipowner who bore the primary obligation to ensure seaworthiness before the voyage commenced,' 'Under no circumstances may the shipowner delegate the seaworthiness obligation to the charterer without express contractual provision.' All structures appear inside texts, not as taught content. New vocabulary (10 words): seaworthiness obligation (the absolute legal duty of a shipowner to ensure the vessel is fit for the intended voyage before and at the commencement of the voyage — distinct from the general seaworthiness concept already taught), cargo worthiness (the condition in which a vessel's holds and fittings are appropriate to receive, carry, and preserve the specific cargo being transported), inherent vice (a quality in the cargo itself that causes it to deteriorate without any external fault — a recognized defense in cargo claims), deviation from voyage (an unauthorized departure from the agreed or customary route that can void the shipowner's liability protection under the bill of lading), general average contribution (the proportional share of a general average loss that each party in a maritime venture is required to pay), hague-visby rules (the international framework governing the liability of carriers for loss or damage to cargo under a bill of lading), carrier liability limit (the maximum financial exposure of a shipowner or carrier for cargo loss under the applicable convention or contract), cargo survey (the formal inspection of cargo condition carried out before loading or after discharge to establish the state of the goods), letter of protest (a formal written notice issued by the master or shipowner objecting to a condition or action that may affect liability), sea protest (a formal sworn statement made by the master before a notary or maritime authority recording the circumstances of a voyage — used as evidence in cargo claims). Revision from Lessons 11, 18, and 24 (3 words): bill of lading, cargo claim, subrogation. Collocations (new): fulfill the seaworthiness obligation, establish cargo worthiness, invoke inherent vice as a defense, authorize a deviation from voyage, conduct a cargo survey. Phrasal verbs in context: set out (the carrier's obligations under the Hague-Visby Rules — twelfth recycling in new liability frame), account for (cargo deterioration — recycled from Lessons 4, 11, 24, and 28 in new inherent vice context), rule out (inherent vice as a defense — recycled from Lessons 9, 18, 24, and 28). Hedging language in legal liability context (recycled from Lesson 9): 'It would appear that the seaworthiness obligation had not been satisfied at the commencement of the voyage,' 'One could argue that the deviation from voyage voided the carrier's liability protection under the Hague-Visby Rules,' 'To some extent, the cargo survey may not have been carried out with sufficient thoroughness.' Exam skill focus: cargo documentation and shipowner liability texts in ASON combine the maximum density of multi-party attribution, temporal sequencing, and term-of-art vocabulary in a single reading set. This lesson builds Helena's ability to slow her reading speed on legal-operational texts — the opposite of the skimming strategy appropriate for procedural texts — and to apply term-of-art disambiguation (introduced in Lesson 24) to a new liability vocabulary set. The specific exam skill practiced is distinguishing between what the bill of lading states, what the Hague-Visby Rules require, and what the court or surveyor found — a three-layer document discrimination task parallel to the MARPOL and MLC layer-discrimination skills built in Lessons 21 and 23.

tema: Block 6 Consolidation and Pre-Final Exam Strategic Assessment — Full ASON Simulation Covering Navigational Authority, Port Operations, COLREGS Applications, and Cargo Liability, with Individual Exam-Readiness Diagnostic

The format for each item: (a) the question stem and correct answer; (b) the answer Helena selected; (c) the error type (from the teacher's taxonomy); (d) the specific sentence in the text that supports the correct answer; (e) the grammar structure or vocabulary term that the question was testing; (f) one sentence Helena writes herself using that structure or term in a new context drawn from her target role as a Ship's Pilot. Helena sends this error correction document before Lesson 31 — it becomes the primary input for the teacher's Block 7 lesson design. Task 2 — Personal exam strategy checklist (15 min): Helena writes a personal one-page checklist summarizing the five Block 6 exam strategies in her own words, with one concrete example from a simulation question for each strategy. This checklist is her personal ASON exam reference document — she may add to it in Lessons 31–38 and bring it to her review sessions in the weeks before the March 2027 exam. Task 3 — Targeted vocabulary self-test (15 min): Without referring to notes, Helena writes a one-sentence definition in English and a one-sentence example in formal maritime register for each of the ten Block 6 consolidation vocabulary items (nautical chart, compulsory pilotage, mandatory reporting point, crossing situation, point of closest approach, seaworthiness obligation, inherent vice, deviation from voyage, Hague-Visby Rules, sea protest). She checks her definitions against the lesson vocabulary record and marks any item she could not define accurately for immediate priority revision before Lesson 31. Helena sends this self-test with the error correction document.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and Lead-in (10 min): Teacher and Helena conduct a five-minute spoken review of the five exam strategies consolidated across Block 6. For each strategy, Helena states the strategy name, the text type it targets, and one example from a Lesson 26–29 simulation where she either applied it correctly or needed to correct herself. This verbal activation serves two purposes: it reinforces the strategies as named tools rather than implicit habits, and it gives the teacher a real-time read on Helena's metacognitive confidence before the simulation begins. Teacher briefly reviews the three revision vocabulary items (causal chain, compliance, flag state) and confirms that Helena can place each in at least two of the text-type domains covered in Blocks 5 and 6. Teacher sets the simulation parameters: 15 questions, 45 minutes, no notes, full exam conditions. Simulation (45 min): Helena completes the full 15-question ASON-format simulation independently under timed exam conditions. The simulation is structured as three multi-text sets: Set 1 (5 questions) — SOLAS Chapter V navigational authority combined with a VTS communication log (targeting Lessons 26 and 27 vocabulary and grammar); Set 2 (5 questions) — COLREGS rule extract combined with a collision investigation report and a technical expert opinion (targeting Lesson 28 vocabulary and the three-register grammar integration at program ceiling); Set 3 (5 questions) — a Hague-Visby Rules extract combined with a cargo survey report and a letter of protest (targeting Lesson 29 vocabulary and the conditional-plus-past-perfect grammar integration). Every question type confirmed in ASON 2025 and 2026 is represented: explicit statement identification, inference from hedging language, paraphrase recognition, party-attribution identification, vocabulary in context (two questions), cross-text synthesis (two questions), and register-discrimination. Teacher monitors on screen, takes no notes during the simulation, and does not intervene. Debrief and Diagnostic (25 min): Teacher scores the simulation immediately on screen. For each incorrect answer, teacher labels the error type using the program's established taxonomy: grammar-structure confusion (which structure, which distractor); vocabulary misidentification (which term, which distractor term); party-attribution error (which party was attributed incorrectly); register confusion (which register was confused with which); document-layer confusion (which layer was confused with which). Teacher aggregates the error types across all 15 questions into a written diagnostic summary produced on screen. Helena reads the summary and identifies which of the five Block 6 strategies she applied least consistently. focoLinguistico: Grammar (consolidation — no new structure introduced): Full application of all grammar structures taught across the entire program (Lessons 1–29) inside a timed full-format ASON simulation. Block 6 structures are foregrounded in the question distribution: cleft sentences and relative clauses with party-attribution complexity (Lessons 6 and 26), reported speech with future perfect backshift (Lessons 3 and 27), inversion with three-register expert opinion language (Lessons 5 and 28), past perfect and conditional integration inside liability analysis (Lessons 11, 12, and 29). All structures from Blocks 1 through 5 also circulate: modal perfects full range (Lessons 2 and 13), passive voice and causative (Lesson 4), gerunds vs. infinitives (Lesson 7), future perfect and future continuous (Lesson 8), advanced modals and hedging (Lesson 9), subjunctive (Lesson 10), wish constructions (Lesson 15), used to / be used to / get used to (Lessons 8 and 21). Grammar appears exclusively inside reading texts and answer options — not as taught content. Vocabulary consolidation — Block 6 cumulative review (10 words drawn from the highest-error items across Lessons 26–29, determined by the teacher's aggregated error analysis from the four Production simulations): Default set if error data is insufficient: nautical chart, compulsory pilotage, mandatory reporting point, crossing situation, point of closest approach, seaworthiness obligation, inherent vice, deviation from voyage, Hague-Visby Rules, sea protest — the ten terms most frequently involved in distractor confusion across Block 6 texts. Revision from the full program arc (3 words): causal chain, compliance, flag state — the three anchor terms that connect the navigational, regulatory, crew welfare, and liability domains across the complete program. Exam strategy consolidation for Block 6 — five-strategy integration: (1) four-step resolution and regulation parsing (Lesson 20 method, applied to SOLAS Chapter V and COLREGS in Lessons 26 and 28); (2) register-tracking across three-text sets (regulatory / operational-testimony / legal-expert — introduced in Lesson 28, reinforced in Lesson 29); (3) term-of-art disambiguation at maximum density (Lessons 24 and 29 combined vocabulary set); (4) three-layer document discrimination for liability texts (Hague-Visby Rules / bill of lading / survey report — Lesson 29 strategy); (5) party-attribution accuracy in complex sentences using cleft structures, inversion, and conditional logic simultaneously. The diagnostic note produced at the end of this lesson names Helena's three most consistent residual error patterns, maps each to a specific text type and question format, and prescribes the targeted work for the final two blocks (Lessons 31–38) leading to the exam in March 2027.

tema: Final Stretch — Targeted Remediation of Helena's Three Residual Error Patterns from the Block 6 Diagnostic
homework: Task 1 (25 min): Helena returns to the eight remediation items from the Presentation phase and writes a one-sentence explanation for each wrong distractor — not just why the correct answer is right, but why each incorrect option is wrong and which document layer, party, or grammar structure it misrepresents. She submits this as a typed document in the shared Google Doc before Lesson 32. Task 2 (20 min): Helena selects three sentences from the Lesson 30 simulation texts — one illustrating each of her three error patterns — and rewrites each sentence twice: once paraphrasing without the grammar structure that caused confusion, and once with the grammar structure preserved but the distractor element removed. This produces six sentences that she reads aloud and records as a 4-minute audio file sent to the teacher before Lesson 32. Task 3 (15 min): Helena reviews her personal error log from Lessons 19 through 30 and identifies whether any of her three current error patterns appeared in the Lesson 19 mid-program baseline — a longitudinal self-assessment that connects the Block 7 remediation arc to the full program trajectory. She notes her finding in two sentences at the top of the shared Google Doc.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and lead-in (10 min): Teacher opens the Lesson 30 diagnostic note on shared screen. Helena reads her three identified error patterns aloud. For each pattern, she states in one sentence what the error was and what the correct strategy should have been. This is not a correction exercise — it is a metacognitive activation that primes her attention for the remediation work. Presentation (18 min): Teacher presents eight targeted remediation items drawn from the exact question formats that produced errors in Lesson 30. Items are displayed one at a time. For each, Helena reads the stem and four options silently, selects her answer in the chat, and then the teacher reveals the correct answer with a full elimination commentary — naming which document layer the distractor was drawn from, which party was misattributed, or which modal perfect was substituted. Helena annotates her personal error log in a shared Google Doc as each item is debriefed. Practice (17 min): Helena works through ten new ASON-format items targeting the same three error patterns in fresh texts — two excerpts from ASON 2025 and 2026 papers not previously used in the program. She answers under timed conditions (90 seconds per item) and submits answers in the chat. Teacher tracks response time and flags any item where Helena hesitates more than 60 seconds — hesitation pattern is itself diagnostic data for the Block 7 arc. Production (35 min): Helena completes a 10-question mixed simulation drawn from all three error domains simultaneously, timed to exam conditions. She then conducts a self-scored debrief using the answer key and elimination commentary provided by the teacher. For each item she answered incorrectly, she writes one sentence in the shared doc identifying which of the three error patterns caused the mistake. The session ends with Helena reading her updated personal error log aloud — three patterns, three self-identified corrections, one consolidated elimination protocol stated in her own words. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher confirms which of the three patterns has been resolved and which requires continued attention in Lessons 32 through 35. This confirmation is written into the shared doc as a live planning note visible to Helena — she knows exactly what the next four lessons will prioritize.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (consolidation — no new structure introduced): Direct remediation of the three error patterns identified in the Lesson 30 diagnostic note. Based on confirmed ASON error profiles at this stage, the default remediation targets are: (1) modal perfect discrimination under time pressure — candidates who correctly identify 'should have' vs. 'must have' in isolation but collapse the distinction when embedded inside reported speech or hedging chains ('The investigator concluded that the officer should have altered course' vs. 'The officer must have been unaware of the risk of collision'); (2) party-attribution errors in cleft sentences and inversion when three or more parties appear in a single complex sentence (flag state, recognized organization, port state authority, master); (3) three-layer document discrimination — selecting an answer that accurately represents what the bill of lading states rather than what the Hague-Visby Rules require or what the surveyor found. All three error types are addressed through targeted re-exposure to the specific sentence structures that produced errors in Lesson 30, not through reteaching. Vocabulary (new — 10 words): statutory duty (a legal obligation imposed directly by an international convention or national legislation, as distinct from a contractual obligation); delegated authority (the formal transfer of a regulatory function from a flag state to a recognized organization); port state measure (any formal action taken by a port state in response to a vessel's non-compliance, including detention, expulsion, or referral); certificate of compliance (a document confirming that a vessel meets the requirements of a specific regulation or convention); concurrent jurisdiction (the situation in which two or more states have simultaneous legal authority over the same vessel or incident); preliminary finding (an initial conclusion reached before a full investigation is complete — distinct from formal finding already taught in Lesson 19); liability allocation (the formal distribution of financial responsibility among parties following a maritime casualty); contractual defense (a legal argument arising from the terms of a contract rather than from statute or convention); procedural breach (a failure to follow a required process or step, as distinct from a substantive non-compliance with a rule); evidentiary standard (the level of proof required to establish a fact in a maritime investigation or legal proceeding). Revision from Lessons 18, 22, and 29 (3 words): causal chain, flag state, seaworthiness obligation. Collocations (new): establish concurrent jurisdiction, invoke a contractual defense, apply a statutory duty, allocate liability among parties, meet an evidentiary standard. Phrasal verbs in remediation context (recycled): account for (liability allocation — thirteenth recycling, now in remediation frame); rule out (a contractual defense — recycled from Lessons 9, 18, 24, 28, and 29); set out (a statutory duty — thirteenth recycling). Hedging language in diagnostic remediation context (recycled from Lesson 9, applied to residual error patterns): 'It would appear that the statutory duty had been delegated to a recognized organization prior to the inspection,' 'One could argue that the preliminary finding does not satisfy the evidentiary standard required for a formal finding of liability.' Exam strategy focus: Helena works through eight targeted remediation questions — two per error pattern plus two mixed-pattern items — each derived from the specific question format and distractor structure that produced errors in Lesson 30. For each item, the teacher walks through the elimination sequence: identify the document layer, locate the party, track the grammar structure, eliminate register mismatches. The lesson closes with Helena articulating her own elimination protocol in her own words — a metacognitive consolidation step that converts corrected errors into transferable exam strategy.

tema: Port State Control in Practice — Reading Concentrated Inspection Campaign Reports and Enforcement Action Notices at Full ASON Complexity
homework: Task 1 (20 min): Helena reads one page of the Paris MOU Annual Report (current edition, teacher-provided PDF link) and identifies three sentences containing any of the following structures: modal perfects, cleft sentences, or subjunctive base form. For each sentence, she writes in the shared Google Doc: the full sentence, the grammar structure identified, the party responsible, and whether the sentence states a fact or implies a conclusion. Task 2 (15 min): Helena writes five sentences using the new vocabulary from this lesson — white list, grounds for detention, deficiency code, rectification period, operational restriction — in contexts that replicate ASON text register. Each sentence must contain at least one grammar structure from the program. Sentences are submitted in the shared Google Doc before Lesson 33. Task 3 (10 min): Helena records a 2-minute audio in which she explains, as if briefing a colleague, the difference between a standard PSC inspection and an enhanced inspection under a concentrated inspection campaign, using at least three terms from today's new vocabulary set and at least one hedging expression from Lesson 9.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and lead-in (10 min): Teacher shares on screen a simplified MOU performance table showing three flag states — one on the white list, one on the grey list, one on the black list — with inspection frequency data. Helena reads the table and answers three oral comprehension questions: which flag state is most likely to have its vessels targeted for enhanced inspection, what data point would change a flag state's ranking, and what the difference is between a detention and an operational restriction. This activates prior vocabulary from Lessons 16 and 22 and establishes the PSC ranking system as the lesson's conceptual frame. Presentation (18 min): Teacher displays the two-text set on shared screen — Text A is a concentrated inspection campaign report (two paragraphs: scope and findings), Text B is a formal enforcement action notice issued to a specific vessel. Teacher reads Text A aloud while Helena follows. Teacher then annotates two key sentences on screen: the cleft-plus-subjunctive construction and the reported-speech-plus-modal-perfect chain. For each, Helena identifies the main verb, the party responsible, and the grammar structure involved — a live application of the four-step parsing method. Practice (17 min): Helena answers eight ASON-format questions targeting Texts A and B under timed conditions (90 seconds per item). Questions are distributed across the three current error patterns from Lesson 31: two modal perfect discrimination items, three party-attribution items, and three document-layer items. Teacher tracks response time and notes any item where Helena pauses. After submission, teacher and Helena debrief three items — the one Helena found hardest, the one she answered fastest, and one the teacher selects based on the specific distractor structure most likely to appear in ASON 2027. Production (35 min): Helena completes a 12-question simulation using two new texts from the PSC domain not previously used in the lesson. She answers under full exam conditions — no annotation, no teacher commentary, 90 seconds per item. After scoring, Helena identifies the one item that most closely resembles her Lesson 30 error patterns and writes a three-sentence elimination commentary in the shared Google Doc: what the text stated, which distractor was tempting and why, and which strategy resolved it. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher confirms whether the modal-perfect-plus-reported-speech error pattern from Lesson 30 has been resolved in this lesson's data. If resolved, it is crossed off the shared error log. If not, the teacher prescribes the specific homework task targeting it.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (advanced integration — no new structure introduced): All grammar structures already taught are applied inside a two-text ASON set combining a concentrated inspection campaign report (passive voice, causative, subjunctive base form, relative clauses with prepositions) and a formal enforcement action notice (modal perfects, inversion for emphasis, cleft sentences). The grammar emphasis this lesson is the co-occurrence of subjunctive base form inside an operative paragraph embedded within a cleft sentence — a construction type confirmed in ASON 2026: 'It is the port state authority that requires that all vessels flying flags of convenience demonstrate compliance before entry.' Helena must recognize that the subjunctive base form ('demonstrate') is triggered by 'requires that' inside a cleft sentence, not by the cleft structure itself. Second grammar focus: modal perfects (Lessons 2 and 13) inside PSC enforcement action notices that also contain reported speech (Lesson 3) — 'The inspector reported that the vessel must have been operating without a valid statutory certificate for at least three months.' This reported-speech-plus-modal-perfect chain is the specific construction that produced errors in the Lesson 30 diagnostic and is now targeted in a new PSC text type. Vocabulary (new — 10 words): white list (a ranking of flag states with consistently high PSC performance, maintained by regional MOUs); grey list (a ranking of flag states with intermediate PSC performance, subject to increased inspection frequency); black list (a ranking of flag states with persistently poor PSC performance, resulting in enhanced targeting of their vessels); enhanced inspection (a more intensive PSC examination applied to high-risk vessels, covering additional areas beyond a standard inspection); deficiency code (a standardized numerical code assigned to each type of deficiency found during a PSC inspection); grounds for detention (the legal basis on which a port state authority may hold a vessel in port — safety risk, certificate invalidity, or serious non-compliance); rectification period (the agreed or mandated time within which a shipowner must correct identified deficiencies); advisory notice (a formal communication from a PSC authority to a vessel's flag state informing it of deficiencies found); targeted port (a port specifically designated as a participant in a concentrated inspection campaign); operational restriction (a formal limitation on a vessel's permitted activities imposed by a port state as an alternative to full detention). Revision from Lessons 10, 16, and 22 (3 words): concentrated inspection campaign, detention order, recognized organization. Collocations (new): appear on the black list, conduct an enhanced inspection, assign a deficiency code, establish grounds for detention, issue an advisory notice. Phrasal verbs in context: come under (enhanced inspection — recycled in new PSC campaign frame); phase out (vessels with persistent non-compliance — fourteenth recycling); carry out (a PSC inspection under a concentrated campaign — thirteenth recycling). Hedging language in PSC enforcement register (recycled from Lesson 9): 'It would appear that the flag state's black list status contributed to the vessel being selected for enhanced inspection,' 'To some extent, the rectification period may not have been adequate given the number of deficiencies identified.' Exam strategy focus: concentrated inspection campaign reports combine regulatory language (defining the campaign scope and criteria) with enforcement language (recording specific deficiencies and actions taken) in a single document — Helena practices the four-step parsing method from Lesson 20 applied to this two-section document format, identifying the boundary between the regulatory scope section and the enforcement findings section before answering any question.

tema: Salvage, Wreck Removal, and Environmental Liability — Reading the Nairobi Convention, Wreck Removal Notices, and Insurance Correspondence in a Three-Text ASON Set
homework: Task 1 (25 min): Helena reads Articles 9 and 10 of the Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks (teacher-provided PDF link, two pages) and answers five comprehension questions in the shared Google Doc: (1) What obligation does Article 9 place on the registered owner? (2) What right does the affected state acquire under Article 10? (3) Which party provides the financial security? (4) Is the obligation in Article 9 a statutory duty or a contractual obligation? (5) Write one sentence paraphrasing the core obligation using at least one grammar structure from the program. Task 2 (15 min): Helena identifies five noun phrases from Text C (the P and I Club letter from today's lesson) that she considers potential terms of art — multi-word phrases that carry a precise legal meaning rather than their ordinary English meaning. For each, she writes one sentence explaining what the term means in the maritime legal context and one sentence explaining what a non-specialist reader might incorrectly assume it means. Submitted in the shared Google Doc. Task 3 (10 min): Helena writes three sentences using the new vocabulary — hazard assessment, intervention right, compulsory insurance — in contexts that replicate the register of Text B (a coastal state authority notice). Each sentence must use the subjunctive base form or inversion for emphasis.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and lead-in (10 min): Teacher shares a one-paragraph case summary on screen — a vessel runs aground in a coastal state's exclusive economic zone, the owner is unresponsive, and the state must decide whether to act. Helena reads the summary and answers two questions: who bears primary responsibility under international law, and what document would a P and I Club issue to guarantee the owner's financial obligations. This activates prior vocabulary from Lessons 8, 21, and 24 and frames the Nairobi Convention as the lesson's regulatory anchor. Presentation (18 min): Teacher displays all three texts simultaneously on shared screen using a split-panel layout — Text A (Nairobi Convention extract, six lines), Text B (wreck removal notice, four lines), Text C (P and I Club insurance letter, five lines). Teacher guides Helena through one pass of each text using the four-step parsing method from Lesson 20: identify document type, locate main verb, identify the party responsible, apply states-vs.-implies distinction. For Text C, teacher highlights the two conditional sentences and asks Helena to identify which is third conditional and which is mixed — a direct application of Lesson 12 in new legal-commercial language. Practice (17 min): Helena answers ten ASON-format questions targeting the three-text set. Questions include two items requiring cross-text comparison — a question type confirmed in ASON 2026 in which the correct answer synthesizes information from two different texts. Helena answers under timed conditions and submits via chat. Teacher and Helena debrief the two cross-text comparison items in full — these are the highest-difficulty items in the set and the most likely source of errors. Production (35 min): Helena completes a full 10-question simulation using a new three-text set covering a different casualty scenario in the same domain (a tanker grounding with environmental spill claims). She answers under full exam conditions. After scoring, she writes one paragraph in the shared Google Doc identifying which of the three texts was the source of the most distractor confusion and explaining why — a register-analysis exercise that builds metalinguistic awareness of her own reading process. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher introduces the Lesson 34 domain (flag state investigation reports combined with IMO casualty statistics) as the penultimate complex text type before the final simulation sequence begins in Lesson 35.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (advanced integration — no new structure introduced): The full grammar architecture is applied inside a three-text ASON set — the highest-demand format — combining: Text A, a Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks extract (subjunctive base form, passive voice, operative paragraph structure); Text B, a wreck removal notice issued by a coastal state authority (modal perfects, cleft sentences, inversion for emphasis); Text C, insurance correspondence between a P and I Club and a shipowner regarding salvage costs (reported speech, past perfect, hedging language, conditional logic). This three-text combination has not appeared in any previous lesson and represents a domain — wreck removal and environmental liability — that Helena has encountered only in fragments (salvage in Lesson 8, environmental liability in Lesson 21, insurance in Lesson 24). The lesson integrates all three domains into a unified examination reading set for the first time. Grammar emphasis: third conditional and mixed conditional logic (Lesson 12) inside insurance correspondence — 'If the wreck had been removed within the mandated period, the coastal state would not have exercised its right of intervention' (third conditional); 'If the P and I Club had issued the financial guarantee earlier, the vessel would currently be released from the coastal state's jurisdiction' (mixed: past condition, present consequence). Second grammar emphasis: inversion inside a coastal state authority notice — 'Under no circumstances may the wreck be left in a navigable channel without prior authorization from the competent authority' — distinguishing this from the contractual inversion already taught in Lesson 24. Vocabulary (new — 10 words): wreck (a vessel that has sunk, stranded, or been abandoned and poses a hazard to navigation or the environment); wreck removal (the compulsory or voluntary operation to refloat, remove, or destroy a wreck under the Nairobi Convention); affected state (the coastal state in whose exclusive economic zone or territorial waters a wreck is located); registered owner (the person or company in whose name the vessel is officially registered — the party bearing primary wreck removal liability under the Nairobi Convention); financial security (a guarantee — typically provided by a P and I Club — that a shipowner can meet wreck removal costs); intervention right (the authority of an affected state to carry out wreck removal itself if the registered owner fails to act, and charge costs); hazard assessment (the formal evaluation of whether a wreck constitutes a danger to navigation, the environment, or coastal interests); wreck marking (the obligation to identify and mark a wreck's position with navigational warnings immediately after the casualty); compulsory insurance (the requirement under the Nairobi Convention that vessel owners maintain insurance covering wreck removal liability); cost recovery (the legal mechanism by which an affected state recoups wreck removal expenses from the registered owner or insurer). Revision from Lessons 8, 21, and 24 (3 words): salvage, P and I Club, limitation of liability. Collocations (new): conduct a hazard assessment, provide financial security, exercise the right of intervention, recover wreck removal costs, fulfill the wreck marking obligation. Phrasal verbs in context: carry out (wreck removal — fourteenth recycling in new Nairobi Convention frame); set out (wreck removal obligations — fourteenth recycling); account for (environmental damage costs — recycled from Lessons 4, 11, 24, 28, and 29 in new environmental liability frame). Hedging language in coastal state authority register (recycled from Lesson 9): 'It would appear that the financial security had not been confirmed prior to the coastal state's decision to exercise its right of intervention,' 'To some extent, the delay in hazard assessment may have contributed to the navigational risk posed by the wreck.' Exam strategy focus: the three-text ASON set requires Helena to apply two simultaneous strategies — register-tracking (Text A is regulatory, Text B is authoritative-operational, Text C is commercial-legal) and document-layer identification (Nairobi Convention obligation vs. coastal state notice vs. insurance correspondence). Questions in this format routinely offer answer options that correctly describe what one text states but attribute it to the wrong text. Helena practices flagging the source text for each answer option before selecting.

tema: IMO Casualty Statistics, Flag State Investigation Reports, and the Language of Maritime Safety Trend Analysis — Reading Data-Driven and Investigative Texts Together at ASON Level
homework: Task 1 (30 min): Helena reads one complete flag state investigation report published on the IMO website (teacher-provided direct link to a published report in the IMO casualty database, approximately 4 pages, final findings section only). She identifies and annotates in the shared Google Doc: (a) three sentences using modal perfects, with each modal perfect underlined and the degree of certainty it expresses noted; (b) two instances of hedging language, with each identified as trend-level or individual-causation; (c) one cleft sentence or inversion, with the party being emphasized identified. Task 2 (15 min): Helena writes a five-sentence summary of the investigation report she read, using: past perfect for temporal sequencing (minimum two instances), modal perfects for causal analysis (minimum two instances), and one hedging expression for the overall conclusion. Summary submitted in the shared Google Doc before Lesson 35. Task 3 (10 min): Helena identifies three new vocabulary items from this lesson — casualty rate, causal factor classification, dissemination requirement — and writes one ASON-style question stem for each, with four answer options (one correct, three distractors), replicating the question format she has encountered throughout the program. The three question stems are submitted in the shared Google Doc and will be used as warm-up material in Lesson 35.
atividadeEmAula: Warm-up and lead-in (10 min): Teacher shares on screen a simplified casualty statistics table — three incident categories (collision, grounding, fire), three flag state performance bands (white, grey, black list), and two time periods (2022–2024 and 2024–2026). Helena reads the table and answers three oral questions: which incident category shows the largest increase, which flag state band accounts for the majority of investigation reports, and what causal factor the teacher hypothesizes is driving the trend. This activates the lesson's statistical reading frame without requiring Helena to know the new vocabulary in advance. Presentation (18 min): Teacher displays the two-text set on shared screen — Text A is a four-paragraph flag state investigation report summary (final findings section), Text B is a two-paragraph IMO casualty statistics summary with one embedded table. Teacher guides Helena through a comparative reading pass: for each causal factor mentioned in Text A, Helena identifies whether the same factor appears in Text B, and if so, in which grammatical register. Teacher annotates three instances of cross-register paraphrase — same causal event, different grammar structure — and Helena labels each in the shared Google Doc: modal perfect in Text A, passive subjunctive in Text B, or hedging in both. Practice (17 min): Helena answers ten ASON-format questions targeting the two-text set. Three questions require cross-text comparison, four require distinguishing trend-level hedging from individual-causation hedging, and three test vocabulary from this lesson and Lessons 18 and 19. Helena answers under timed conditions. Teacher debrief focuses on the three cross-text comparison items — the teacher displays both texts simultaneously and walks through the elimination sequence for each item, identifying which distractor was drawing from the wrong text and why it was tempting. Production (35 min): Helena completes a 12-question simulation using a new two-text set — a different flag state investigation report (tanker collision in restricted waters) paired with a different IMO safety recommendation tracking document. Full exam conditions, no commentary. After scoring, Helena writes in the shared Google Doc: one sentence identifying the cross-register paraphrase that appeared in this simulation's most difficult question, and one sentence explaining the elimination strategy she used. Wrap-up (10 min): Teacher previews Lesson 35 as the program's penultimate full simulation — the last opportunity to identify and address any residual error patterns before the final assessment sequence in Lessons 36 through 38. Teacher asks Helena to state, without looking at her error log, the one grammar structure and the one vocabulary domain she is least confident about entering the final simulation. This oral self-assessment becomes the input for the Lesson 35 simulation design.
focoLinguistico: Grammar (advanced integration — no new structure introduced): The lesson targets a two-text ASON set combining a flag state investigation report (modal perfects, reported speech, past perfect, hedging language — the grammar density last seen at this level in Lesson 28) with an IMO casualty statistics summary (passive voice, subjunctive, cleft sentences — a text type in which quantitative data is presented in formal regulatory prose). The specific grammar challenge introduced in this pairing is that the same causal event is described in two registers simultaneously: the investigation report uses hedged modal perfects ('The investigation concluded that the officer must have been fatigued') while the IMO statistics text uses formal passive with subjunctive recommendations ('It is recommended that member states ensure that crew rest hours be monitored'). Helena must track that both texts are referring to the same causal factor — crew fatigue — while using completely different grammatical structures to express it. This cross-register paraphrase recognition is the most demanding form of inference question in ASON multi-text sets. Grammar emphasis: hedging language discrimination (Lesson 9) applied at maximum density — the casualty statistics text uses hedging to describe industry trends ('It would appear that the rate of collision incidents has increased in restricted waterways over the past three years') while the investigation report uses hedging to describe individual causation ('It seems that the officer may not have been aware of the vessel's deviation from the approved route'). Helena must distinguish trend-level hedging from individual-causation hedging when both appear in the same question set — a confirmed ASON 2026 error pattern.
